brief.en: Adversaries may obfuscate command and control traffic to make it more difficult to detect. Command and control (C2) communications are hidden (but not necessarily encrypted) in an attempt to make the content more difficult to discover or decipher and to make the communication less conspicuous and hide commands from being seen.

description.en: Detects excessive outbound traffic to remote host over HTTP(S) from uncommon or previously unseen processes.

mutableElements.description: Defines threshold ratio of outbound to inbound bytes that signals possible obfuscation
List of known legitimate network clients to exclude from anomaly checks

description.en: Identifies custom or previously unseen userland processes initiating high-volume HTTP connections with low response volume.

mutableElements.description: Defines what is considered abnormal for a user-initiated process context

description.en: Flags unexpected user applications initiating long-lived HTTP(S) sessions with irregular traffic patterns.

mutableElements.description: Session length that exceeds average per-user expectations

brief.en: Adversaries may add junk data to protocols used for command and control to make detection more difficult. By adding random or meaningless data to the protocols used for command and control, adversaries can prevent trivial methods for decoding, deciphering, or otherwise analyzing the traffic. Examples may include appending/prepending data with junk characters or writing junk characters between significant characters.

description.en: Processes generating large outbound connections with disproportionate send/receive ratios, often to uncommon ports or hosts, potentially inserting meaningless data into protocol payloads.

mutableElements.description: Tunable threshold for Shannon entropy of network payloads.
Duration of outbound data transfer to evaluate disproportionate upload size.
Filter based on user accounts allowed to generate outbound traffic.

description.en: Outbound traffic with anomalous payload sizes and patterns from non-networking processes, often observed via packet inspection or connection logs.

mutableElements.description: Adjust based on expected entropy of typical outbound data.
Exclude known good binaries that generate high network output.
Minimum ratio of bytessent to bytesreceived.

description.en: Previously unseen applications generating outbound connections with atypical data flow characteristics, such as excessive data with no return response.

mutableElements.description: Allow filtering based on parent-child relationship for benign services.
Known legitimate C2-like patterns (e.g., Apple telemetry).

description.en: Anomalous traffic from ESXi host management daemons (like hostd or vpxa) embedding non-standard payloads in management protocols (e.g., HTTPS) or beaconing behavior.

mutableElements.description: Detects mismatched TLS client behavior vs expected for hostd/vpxa.
Highlight traffic from ESXi hosts to uncommon ports outside vCenter ranges.

brief.en: Adversaries may use steganographic techniques to hide command and control traffic to make detection efforts more difficult. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital messages that are transferred between systems. This hidden information can be used for command and control of compromised systems.

description.en: Detect the creation or modification of common media file formats (e.g., .jpg, .png, .wav) following suspicious process activity like compression or encryption, especially when paired with lateral movement or exfiltration behavior.

mutableElements.description: Allows tuning of monitored file types (e.g., .jpg, .png, .docx).
Threshold for flagging potential hidden data in outbound payloads.
Time window between media creation and network transmission.

description.en: Unusual use of steganographic or media processing binaries (e.g., steghide, ffmpeg, imagemagick) followed by outbound communication to external IPs with high data output and media MIME types.

mutableElements.description: Specify which binaries to monitor (e.g., steghide, outguess).
Adjust based on known normal file upload services.

description.en: Abnormal usage of Preview, ImageMagick, or binary editors to alter images/documents, followed by exfiltration or outbound connections with mismatched file MIME types or payload structure.

mutableElements.description: Allow tuning based on expected apps calling image-editing tools.
Gap between file manipulation and outbound connection.

description.en: Suspicious modification of file artifacts (e.g., logs, ISO templates) on ESXi datastores, followed by beaconing or POST operations to external IPs potentially hiding payloads in file-like traffic.

mutableElements.description: Tune for likely stego file names (e.g., wallpaper.jpg, template.iso).
Destination outside vCenter management subnet.

brief.en: Adversaries may impersonate legitimate protocols or web service traffic to disguise command and control activity and thwart analysis efforts. By impersonating legitimate protocols or web services, adversaries can make their command and control traffic blend in with legitimate network traffic.

description.en: Untrusted processes creating outbound TLS/HTTPS connections with malformed certificates or header fields, often mismatched with target service behavior. Detects protocol impersonation attempts via traffic metadata analysis and host process lineage.

mutableElements.description: Organizations in certificate issuer fields to allowlist or monitor.
Restrict detection to non-system users or external-facing applications.
Specific HTTP header anomalies or patterns (e.g., missing User-Agent).

description.en: Detection of binaries spawning encrypted sessions using OpenSSL or curl to external services with mismatched ports/protocols. Identifies behavior where internal services simulate trusted cloud service traffic patterns.

mutableElements.description: Threshold for header-field mismatch against expected service behavior.
Correlation window between process spawn and encrypted session.

description.en: Unsigned or suspicious applications initiating network traffic claiming to be browser, mail, or cloud clients. Detects impersonation via TLS fingerprint and User-Agent string deviation.

mutableElements.description: Limit detections to children of suspicious binaries.
Threshold for deviation from expected headers (User-Agent, Host).

description.en: ESXi hosts initiating connections from non-standard daemons mimicking HTTP/HTTPS or SNMP traffic, but with irregular payload formats or expired/unsigned TLS certificates.

mutableElements.description: Allows matching against known-good or known-bad JA3/JA3S hashes.
Tune for expected network ports per ESXi role.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to access credential material stored in the process memory of the Local Security Authority Subsystem Service (LSASS). After a user logs on, the system generates and stores a variety of credential materials in LSASS process memory. These credential materials can be harvested by an administrative user or SYSTEM and used to conduct Lateral Movement using Use Alternate Authentication Material.

description.en: A non-privileged or abnormal process attempts to open a handle with full access (0x1F0FFF) to lsass.exe and subsequently invokes memory dump, file creation, or registry modification indicative of credential scraping. This behavior chain reflects staged credential theft activity.

mutableElements.description: Set to 0x1F0FFF to detect full memory access attempts; can be scoped down to reduce noise.
Defines time between LSASS access and dump file creation or registry modification (e.g., 5 minutes).
Allowlist known legitimate tools (e.g., AV/EDR) accessing lsass.exe.
Paths where memory dumps are written, e.g., %TEMP%, C:\Windows\Temp.
Common dumping syntax like rundll32, procdump, comsvcs.dll, Invoke-Mimikatz.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to extract credential material from the Security Account Manager (SAM) database either through in-memory techniques or through the Windows Registry where the SAM database is stored. The SAM is a database file that contains local accounts for the host, typically those found with the net user command. Enumerating the SAM database requires SYSTEM level access.

description.en: An adversary running with SYSTEM-level privileges executes commands or accesses registry keys to dump the SAM hive or directly reads sensitive local files from the config directory. This behavior often involves sequential access to HKLM\SAM, HKLM\SYSTEM, and creation of .save or .dmp files, enabling offline hash extraction.

mutableElements.description: Detectable variations include reg save, reg.exe save, or PowerShell equivalents for dumping SAM/SYSTEM hives.
Defenders can tune based on dump file path patterns (e.g., %TEMP%\sam.save, C:\Users\Public\.dmp).
Tune for HKLM\SAM, HKLM\SYSTEM or access via direct \Device\Harddisk paths.
Temporal gap between SAM and SYSTEM hive dumping can be tuned (e.g., 3 minutes).
Useful for suppressing known-good access (e.g., backup tools).

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to access or create a copy of the Active Directory domain database in order to steal credential information, as well as obtain other information about domain members such as devices, users, and access rights. By default, the NTDS file (NTDS.dit) is located in %SystemRoot%\NTDS\Ntds.dit of a domain controller.

description.en: Detects credential dumping attempts targeting the NTDS.dit database by monitoring shadow copy creation, suspicious file access to %SystemRoot%\NTDS\ntds.dit, and the use of tooling like ntdsutil.exe or volume management APIs.

mutableElements.description: Tunable for NTDS file location or backup paths if organization uses custom domain controller storage structure.
Can suppress backup-related parent processes to reduce false positives.
Temporal correlation between shadow copy creation and NTDS file access (e.g., 5 min window).
Tune based on expected privileged user/service account behavior.

brief.en: Adversaries with SYSTEM access to a host may attempt to access Local Security Authority (LSA) secrets, which can contain a variety of different credential materials, such as credentials for service accounts. LSA secrets are stored in the registry at HKEYLOCALMACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets. LSA secrets can also be dumped from memory. Reg can be used to extract from the Registry.

description.en: Detects adversary activity aimed at accessing LSA Secrets, including registry key export of HKEYLOCALMACHINE\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets or memory scraping via tools such as Mimikatz or PowerSploit's Invoke-Mimikatz.

mutableElements.description: Target registry paths like HKLM\SECURITY\Policy\Secrets or variants can be tuned depending on OS version or registry redirection settings.
Module names such as lsasrv.dll, sechost.dll, or suspicious DLLs loaded by user processes may require tuning for known-good service operations.
Tuning based on whether processes are using specific sensitive access rights (e.g., 0x2 or 0x4).
Temporal window between registry access and command-line tool execution.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to access cached domain credentials used to allow authentication to occur in the event a domain controller is unavailable. On Windows Vista and newer, the hash format is DCC2 (Domain Cached Credentials version 2) hash, also known as MS-Cache v2 hash. The number of default cached credentials varies and can be altered per system.

description.en: Detects adversary behavior accessing Windows cached domain credential files using tools like Mimikatz, reg.exe, or PowerShell, often combined with registry exports or LSASS memory scraping.

mutableElements.description: Location of cached credential files may vary with OS version or custom registry hive exports.
Patterns for reg save, secretsdump, or PowerShell dumping tools may be tuned to org-specific tooling.
Temporal correlation window between process execution and registry/file access.

description.en: Detects access to SSSD or Quest VAS cached credential databases using tdbdump or other file access patterns, requiring sudo/root access.

mutableElements.description: SSSD and Quest cache paths differ by deployment and OS variant.
Tunable to capture specific tools (e.g., tdbdump, cat) or scripts accessing cache files.
Time between elevation and file access can be adjusted to account for legitimate system behavior.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to access credentials and other sensitive information by abusing a Windows Domain Controller's application programming interface (API) to simulate the replication process from a remote domain controller using a technique called DCSync.

description.en: Detects unauthorized invocation of replication operations (DCSync) via Directory Replication Service (DRS), often executed by threat actors using Mimikatz or similar tools from non-DC endpoints.

mutableElements.description: Defines the correlation window for unusual account access followed by DRSUAPI traffic.
Allows tuning for specific accounts known to legitimately request replication.
Expected replication should only come from known DCs; this field allows excluding trusted DCs.

brief.en: Adversaries may gather credentials from the proc filesystem or /proc. The proc filesystem is a pseudo-filesystem used as an interface to kernel data structures for Linux based systems managing virtual memory. For each process, the /proc/<PID>/maps file shows how memory is mapped within the process’s virtual address space.

description.en: Monitoring adversary access to sensitive process memory via the /proc filesystem to extract credential material, often involving multi-step access to /proc/[pid]/mem or /proc/[pid]/maps combined with privilege escalation or credential scraping binaries.

mutableElements.description: Monitored paths such as /proc/[pid]/mem or /proc/[pid]/maps may need to be scoped based on environment
Command-line or binary names associated with credential scraping tools may vary
Elevated user or unexpected user context accessing other process memory may indicate malicious activity
Correlating memory access with process creation or ptrace activity within a specific time range

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to dump the contents of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to enable offline password cracking. Most modern Linux operating systems use a combination of /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow to store user account information, including password hashes in /etc/shadow. By default, /etc/shadow is only readable by the root user.

description.en: Adversaries attempt to read sensitive files such as /etc/passwd and /etc/shadow for credential dumping. This may involve access to the files directly via command-line utilities (e.g., cat, less), creation of backup copies, or parsing through post-exploitation frameworks. Multi-event correlation includes elevated process execution, file access/read on sensitive paths, and anomalous read behaviors tied to non-root or unusual users.

mutableElements.description: Executable name used to access credentials (e.g., cat, cp, awk); can vary across environments
User context under which the access occurs; typically root, but can be non-standard in attacks
Target file paths (e.g., /etc/passwd, /etc/shadow); may vary in containerized or customized systems
Time correlation threshold for chaining access and execution events

brief.en: Adversaries may search local system sources, such as file systems, configuration files, local databases, virtual machine files, or process memory, to find files of interest and sensitive data prior to Exfiltration. Adversaries may do this using a Command and Scripting Interpreter, such as cmd as well as a Network Device CLI, which have functionality to interact with the file system to gather information.

description.en: Adversaries collecting local files via PowerShell, WMI, or direct file API calls often include recursive file listings, targeted file reads, and temporary file staging.

mutableElements.description: Allows tuning for file extensions or paths of sensitive data (e.g., .xls, .db, .pdf).
Used to scope monitoring to suspicious parent/child process trees like PowerShell or WMI spawning file reads.

description.en: Adversaries using bash scripts or tools to recursively enumerate user home directories, config files, or SSH keys.

mutableElements.description: Time span to correlate multiple file access events indicative of scripted or bulk access.
List of tools (e.g., find, grep, tar, scp) that may be benign but are context-sensitive.

description.en: Adversary use of bash/zsh or AppleScript to locate files and exfil targets like user keychains or documents.

mutableElements.description: Useful for excluding known admin or scheduled jobs.
Focus monitoring on removable drives or external paths.

description.en: Collection of device configuration via CLI commands (e.g., show running-config, copy flash, more), often followed by TFTP/SCP transfers.

mutableElements.description: Defines list of configuration or diagnostic commands to monitor.
Helps reduce false positives by whitelisting known admins.

description.en: Adversaries accessing datastore or configuration files via vim-cmd, esxcli, or SCP to extract logs, VMs, or host configurations.

mutableElements.description: Regex for filtering targeted VM paths or files like .vmdk, .vmx.
Tune to distinguish between interactive and script-driven data access.

brief.en: Adversaries may directly access a volume to bypass file access controls and file system monitoring. Windows allows programs to have direct access to logical volumes. Programs with direct access may read and write files directly from the drive by analyzing file system data structures. This technique may bypass Windows file access controls as well as file system monitoring tools.

description.en: Processes accessing raw logical drives (e.g., \.\C:) to bypass file system protections or directly manipulate data structures.

mutableElements.description: Regex pattern to detect access to raw disk volumes like \Device\HarddiskVolume or \.\PhysicalDrive.
Tune for known tools/scripts (e.g., powershell.exe, cmd.exe) often used in misuse scenarios.
Correlate file access and creation across a short time window to avoid false positives.

description.en: CLI or automated utilities accessing raw device volumes or flash storage directly (e.g., via copy flash:, format, or partition commands).

mutableElements.description: Limit detection to volume-level commands (e.g., format, copy, mount, erase).
Filter by internal vs. removable volume interactions (e.g., flash, SD card).

brief.en: Adversaries may try to gather information about registered local system services. Adversaries may obtain information about services using tools as well as OS utility commands such as sc query, tasklist /svc, systemctl --type=service, and net start. Adversaries may also gather information about schedule tasks via commands such as schtasks on Windows or crontab -l on Linux and macOS.

description.en: Enumeration of services via native CLI tools (e.g., sc query, tasklist /svc, net start) or API calls via PowerShell and WMI.

mutableElements.description: Can be tuned to specific binaries used for service enumeration (e.g., sc.exe, tasklist.exe).
Filters for variations like sc query, net start, Get-Service.
Used to suppress known admin scripts or automation jobs.

description.en: Execution of service management commands like systemctl list-units, service --status-all, or direct reading of /etc/init.d.

mutableElements.description: Includes service enumeration commands like systemctl, service, or custom scripts.
Tunable by user context (e.g., root vs. standard user).
Used for correlation with privilege escalation or lateral movement.

description.en: Discovery via launchctl commands, or process enumeration using ps aux | grep com.apple. to identify daemons and services.

mutableElements.description: Tune to recognize launchctl list, launchctl print, or service grep strings.
Filter known benign automation or MDM agent invocations.

brief.en: Adversaries may use fallback or alternate communication channels if the primary channel is compromised or inaccessible in order to maintain reliable command and control and to avoid data transfer thresholds.

description.en: Establishing network connections on uncommon ports or protocols following C2 disruption or blocking. Often executed by processes that typically exhibit no network activity.

mutableElements.description: Can be tuned to include unexpected or high-entropy ports not typically associated with the process.
Useful to filter benign applications vs suspicious fallback attempts.
Tunable ratio of sent/received bytes to indicate potential C2 beaconing or exfiltration.
Adjust temporal window to match likely fallback C2 retries after primary channel fails.

description.en: Creation of outbound connections on alternate ports or using covert transport (e.g., ICMP, DNS) from non-network-intensive processes, following known disruption or blocked traffic.

mutableElements.description: Can filter for rare fallback channel types (e.g., ICMP, DNS over HTTP).
Tuning by user (e.g., root vs. service account) helps suppress noise.

description.en: Outbound fallback traffic from low-profile or background launch agents using unusual protocols or destinations after primary channel inactivity.

mutableElements.description: Used to suppress known legitimate agents.
Can help isolate covert or encrypted fallback traffic.

description.en: Outbound traffic from host management services or guest-to-host interactions over unusual interfaces (e.g., backdoor API endpoints or external VPN tunnels).

mutableElements.description: May vary based on ESXi build and should be filtered to suppress known interfaces.
Environment-specific ranges to ignore (e.g., DR tunnels or out-of-band mgmt).

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of open application windows. Window listings could convey information about how the system is used. For example, information about application windows could be used identify potential data to collect as well as identifying security tooling (Security Software Discovery) to evade. Adversaries typically abuse system features for this type of enumeration.

description.en: Processes using Win32 API calls (e.g., EnumWindows, GetForegroundWindow) or scripting tools (e.g., PowerShell, VBScript) to enumerate open windows. These often appear with reconnaissance or data collection TTPs.

mutableElements.description: Tune to focus on suspicious function calls (e.g., user32.dll!EnumWindows).
Detect behavior from non-interactive or low-privileged users where enumeration is uncommon.
Shorten detection scope to rapid successive window enumeration attempts.

description.en: Scripted or binary usage of X11 utilities (e.g., xdotool, wmctrl) or direct /proc//window mappings to discover open GUI windows and active desktops.

mutableElements.description: Common window management utilities can be tuned to reduce noise (e.g., xprop, xwininfo).
Restrict detection to processes executing under graphical sessions (e.g., DISPLAY=:0).

description.en: Processes that utilize AppleScript, CGWindowListCopyWindowInfo, or NSRunningApplication APIs to list active application windows and foreground processes.

mutableElements.description: Tunable to ignore benign scripting like automation by known apps.
Useful to suppress expected automation processes.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over a different network medium than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, the exfiltration may occur, for example, over a WiFi connection, modem, cellular data connection, Bluetooth, or another radio frequency (RF) channel.

description.en: Execution of file transfer or network access activity through non-primary interfaces (e.g., WiFi, Bluetooth, cellular) by processes not typically associated with such behavior (e.g., rundll32, powershell, regsvr32).

mutableElements.description: Filter for specific interface categories (e.g., WiFi, Bluetooth, 4G).
Tunable for environment-specific large file access events pre-transfer.
Temporal correlation window for file read followed by network activity.

description.en: Use of rfkill, nmcli, or low-level tools (e.g., iw, hcitool, pppd) to enable alternate interfaces followed by data transfer via non-primary NICs.

mutableElements.description: Match known interface manipulation utilities or driver invocations.
Tunable to non-default or rarely used interfaces (e.g., wlan1, hci0).

description.en: AppleScript or system calls to activate WiFi/Bluetooth interfaces (networksetup, blueutil), followed by exfiltration via AirDrop, cloud sync, or network socket.

mutableElements.description: Protocol used for exfil (e.g., AirDrop, mDNS, Apple File Service).
Time period between interface activation and transfer.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to exfiltrate data over Bluetooth rather than the command and control channel. If the command and control network is a wired Internet connection, an adversary may opt to exfiltrate data using a Bluetooth communication channel. Adversaries may choose to do this if they have sufficient access and proximity.

description.en: Detection of non-interactive or suspicious processes accessing Bluetooth interfaces and transmitting outbound traffic following file access or staging activity.

mutableElements.description: Defines how quickly a file access and Bluetooth activity must occur to be correlated.
May focus on Bluetooth-specific interfaces or drivers like 'bthport.sys'.
Tune to trigger only on significant exfiltratable file reads.

description.en: Use of hcitool, bluetoothctl, or rfcomm to initialize Bluetooth connection paired with recent file reads by the same user or session.

mutableElements.description: List of CLI tools to monitor (e.g., hcitool, rfcomm, obexftp).
Amount of time after interface config a file must be accessed to be linked.

description.en: Observation of blueutil/networksetup commands or low-level APIs toggling Bluetooth or initiating transfers, especially if paired with recent large file read activity by non-GUI processes.

mutableElements.description: Limit to background processes or scripts with no GUI interaction.
Focus on specific sensitive file types (e.g., zip, docx, keychain db).

brief.en: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry to gather information about the system, configuration, and installed software. The Registry contains a significant amount of information about the operating system, configuration, software, and security. Information can easily be queried using the Reg utility, though other means to access the Registry exist.

description.en: Registry read access associated with suspicious or non-interactive processes querying system config, installed software, or security settings.

mutableElements.description: Focus detection on registry hives or keys likely to reveal environment info (e.g., HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Windows NT\CurrentVersion).
May tune for suspicious parent processes such as cmd.exe, wscript.exe, or mshta.exe.
Controls how closely registry access must follow process creation for correlation.

brief.en: Adversaries may use rootkits to hide the presence of programs, files, network connections, services, drivers, and other system components. Rootkits are programs that hide the existence of malware by intercepting/hooking and modifying operating system API calls that supply system information.

description.en: Unauthorized or anomalous loading of kernel-mode drivers or DLLs, concealed services, or abnormal modification of boot components indicative of rootkit activity.

mutableElements.description: Signed vs unsigned drivers; many environments restrict unsigned drivers, but some legacy systems allow them.
Suspicious driver or DLL drop locations, e.g., \System32\Drivers\ or \Temp\
Rootkit installation via admin or SYSTEM account.

description.en: Abnormal loading of kernel modules, direct tampering with /dev, /proc, or LDPRELOAD behaviors hiding processes or files.

mutableElements.description: Directories where kernel modules or tampering could be staged (e.g., /lib/modules/).
Regex or heuristic match to anomalous module names (e.g., suspicious entropy or gibberish).
Monitor presence of suspicious preload values that mask processes or files.

description.en: Execution of unsigned kernel extensions (KEXTs), tampering with LaunchDaemons, or userspace hooks into system libraries.

mutableElements.description: Allowable level of unsigned/3rd-party kernel extensions varies by organization.
Detect whether the extension was loaded by an untrusted process or non-root user.
Detection tuned based on deviation from known/approved LaunchDaemon plist files.

brief.en: Adversaries may look for details about the network configuration and settings, such as IP and/or MAC addresses, of systems they access or through information discovery of remote systems. Several operating system administration utilities exist that can be used to gather this information. Examples include Arp, ipconfig/ifconfig, nbtstat, and route.

description.en: Execution of built-in tools (e.g., ipconfig, route, netsh) or PowerShell/WMI queries to enumerate IP, MAC, interface status, or routing configuration.

mutableElements.description: Filter known/legit CLI chains (e.g., explorer.exe → cmd.exe) to reduce FP
Target executions by non-admin or unexpected users
Cluster enumeration commands within short time windows

description.en: Execution of ifconfig, ip a, or access to /proc/net/ indicating collection of local interface and route configuration.

mutableElements.description: Match regex for variations in enumeration syntax (e.g., ip -4 addr show)
Differentiate scripted versus interactive sessions

description.en: Execution of ifconfig, networksetup, or systemprofiler to query IP/MAC/interface configuration and status.

mutableElements.description: Scripted tools (e.g., bash calling ifconfig) vs GUI-initiated inspection
Enumerations executed frequently or across multiple interfaces may indicate enumeration loops

description.en: Use of esxcli network commands (e.g., esxcli network nic list, esxcli network ip interface ipv4 get) via SSH or hostd to enumerate adapter and IP information.

mutableElements.description: Detection may vary based on internal vs remote terminal usage
Distinguish between benign status checks and deep enumeration chains

description.en: CLI-based execution of interface and routing discovery commands (e.g., show ip interface, show arp, show route) over Telnet, SSH, or console.

mutableElements.description: Highlight low-privileged or non-routine users performing discovery
Allow for tuning based on command regex or frequency
SSH vs Telnet vs Console session logging scope

brief.en: Adversaries may check for Internet connectivity on compromised systems. This may be performed during automated discovery and can be accomplished in numerous ways such as using Ping, tracert, and GET requests to websites, or performing initial speed testing to confirm bandwidth.

description.en: Execution of utilities (e.g., ping, tracert, Test-NetConnection) or scripted methods to test Internet connectivity by interacting with external IPs/domains.

mutableElements.description: Tunable external IP ranges or domains used to verify Internet access (e.g., 8.8.8.8, example.com)
Cluster rapid test connections with command execution in < 60 seconds
Filter out known admin/script contexts to reduce false positives

description.en: Execution of ping, traceroute, or curl/wget against public IPs/domains to verify Internet reachability.

mutableElements.description: Regex for common test domains like example.com, google.com
Adjust focus to ICMP, HTTP, or mixed protocol testing

description.en: Execution of ping, traceroute, or network utility tools to external destinations; may include scutil or systemprofiler.

mutableElements.description: Rare use of ICMP utilities may be tuned based on user/host baselines
Tune data joins with parent process and user activity context

description.en: Execution of ping, vmkping, or curl from shell or through automation jobs/scripts to verify Internet egress.

mutableElements.description: Distinguish external SSH sessions from internal admin maintenance
Egress test destination may be filtered to known CDNs/test nodes

brief.en: Adversaries may search for information about Wi-Fi networks, such as network names and passwords, on compromised systems. Adversaries may use Wi-Fi information as part of Account Discovery, Remote System Discovery, and other discovery or Credential Access activity to support both ongoing and future campaigns. Adversaries may collect various types of information about Wi-Fi networks from hosts.

description.en: Enumeration of saved Wi-Fi profiles and cleartext password retrieval using netsh wlan or API-level access to wlanAPI.dll.

mutableElements.description: Filter by known saved SSID names to reduce benign usage of network diagnostics
Anomalous parent-child relationships may be used to spot abuse (e.g., Office → netsh)
Correlate profile enumeration and password dumping within short timeframe (e.g., 60 seconds)

description.en: File access to NetworkManager connection configs and attempts to read PSK credentials from /etc/NetworkManager/system-connections/.

mutableElements.description: Filter for filenames like .nmconnection or profiles containing SSID names
Distinguish between root/admin script usage vs. non-privileged terminal access

description.en: Use of the security command or Keychain API to extract known Wi-Fi passwords for target SSIDs.

mutableElements.description: Match suspicious SSIDs being queried via security find-generic-password -wa
Monitor root/admin usage of credential tools not linked to UI/system processes

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to get a listing of other systems by IP address, hostname, or other logical identifier on a network that may be used for Lateral Movement from the current system. Functionality could exist within remote access tools to enable this, but utilities available on the operating system could also be used such as Ping, net view using Net, or, on ESXi servers, esxcli network diag ping.

description.en: Execution of network enumeration utilities (e.g., net.exe, ping.exe, tracert.exe) in short succession, often chained with lateral movement tools or system enumeration commands.

mutableElements.description: Define bursty execution patterns of enumeration commands (e.g., <30s)
Tunable per org’s scripting/IT tools (e.g., exclude SCCM, PsExec)
Flag suspicious process ancestry (e.g., Word.exe spawning net.exe)

description.en: Use of bash scripts or interactive shells to issue sequential ping, arp, or traceroute commands to map remote hosts.

mutableElements.description: Tune for sensitive internal segments or known lateral targets
Distinguish user-interactive enumeration vs. cronjob or baseline tooling

description.en: Execution of built-in or AppleScript-based system enumeration via arp, netstat, ping, and discovery of /etc/hosts contents.

mutableElements.description: Limit detection to suspicious users or automation contexts
Adapt for expected enumeration tooling used in IT

description.en: ESXi shell or SSH access issuing esxcli network diag ping or viewing routing tables to identify connected hosts.

mutableElements.description: Match specific diag/debug commands abused for recon
Detect unauthorized shell use or user context (e.g., root over SSH)

description.en: Execution of discovery commands like show cdp neighbors, show arp, and other interface-level introspection on Cisco or Juniper devices.

logSources.name: networkdevice:syslog
logSources.channel: syslog facility LOCAL7 or trap messages

mutableElements.description: Device-specific recon commands to monitor based on make/model
Trigger detection for privilege escalation prior to recon commands

brief.en: Adversaries may exfiltrate data, such as sensitive documents, through the use of automated processing after being gathered during Collection. When automated exfiltration is used, other exfiltration techniques likely apply as well to transfer the information out of the network, such as Exfiltration Over C2 Channel and Exfiltration Over Alternative Protocol.

description.en: Detection of automated tools or scripts periodically transmitting data to external destinations using scheduled tasks or background processes.

mutableElements.description: Used to detect repeated exfil activity over intervals (e.g., every 5 minutes).
Can be tuned to filter known internal or trusted destinations.

description.en: Background scripts (e.g., via cron) or daemons transmitting data repeatedly to remote IPs or URLs.

mutableElements.description: Tunable time range for recurring tasks seen creating outbound connections.
Tunable for scope — service accounts vs user accounts.

description.en: Observation of LaunchAgents or LaunchDaemons establishing periodic external connections indicative of automated data transfer.

mutableElements.description: Frequency of task recurrence linked to external communication.
Port number used for detection filtering.

brief.en: Adversaries may leverage traffic mirroring in order to automate data exfiltration over compromised infrastructure. Traffic mirroring is a native feature for some devices, often used for network analysis. For example, devices may be configured to forward network traffic to one or more destinations for analysis by a network analyzer or other monitoring device.

description.en: Configuration changes to virtual TAP/mirror policies that forward traffic to unapproved destinations. Detection correlates management plane API calls with mirrored traffic observation.

logSources.name: AWS:VPCFlowLogs
logSources.channel: Traffic observed on mirror destination instance

mutableElements.description: Detect mirror session creation followed by mirrored traffic within X seconds (e.g., 60s)
Define suspicious or external mirror targets (e.g., non-enterprise ranges)
Flag traffic mirror activity by non-privileged or unexpected IAM roles

description.en: Unauthorized mirroring sessions initiated on routers/switches (e.g., via monitor session, mirror port) coupled with outbound traffic from mirrored interface to unexpected destinations.

logSources.name: networkdevice:Flow
logSources.channel: Traffic from mirrored interface to mirror target IP

mutableElements.description: Tune based on accepted interface config changes (e.g., audit only mirror session creation)
Define high-risk ports used for exfil (e.g., 4443, 8443, 2055)
Define whether mirroring is expected on edge vs core vs distribution devices

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into a computer using the Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user. Remote desktop is a common feature in operating systems. It allows a user to log into an interactive session with a system desktop graphical user interface on a remote system.

description.en: Remote Desktop (RDP) logon by a user followed by unusual process execution, file access, or lateral movement activity within a short timeframe.

mutableElements.description: Temporal threshold to correlate login with post-login activity (e.g., 5 minutes)
Tune for non-admin users or service accounts expected to use RDP
Define suspicious post-login processes such as cmd.exe, powershell.exe, certutil.exe
Scope detection to uncommon or first-time access between source and destination hosts

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with a remote network share using Server Message Block (SMB). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user. SMB is a file, printer, and serial port sharing protocol for Windows machines on the same network or domain. Adversaries may use SMB to interact with file shares, allowing them to move laterally throughout a network.

description.en: An SMB-based remote file share access followed by lateral movement actions such as remote service creation, task scheduling, or suspicious process execution on the target host using ADMIN$ or C$ shares.

mutableElements.description: Targeted admin share path, such as C$, ADMIN$, IPC$
Correlation window between remote file access and remote execution (e.g., 5-10 minutes)
Distinguish expected remote administrators vs. rare/first-time access by specific users
List of suspicious binaries or tools executed post remote copy (e.g., cmd.exe, powershell.exe, runonce.exe)

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote machines by taking advantage of Distributed Component Object Model (DCOM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user.

description.en: A remote DCOM invocation by a privileged account using RPC (port 135), followed by abnormal process instantiation or module loading on the remote system indicative of code execution.

mutableElements.description: Correlate RPC activity with remote process creation within a configurable time window (e.g., 300s)
Identify rare or first-time DCOM invocations by specific accounts
List of suspicious executables commonly abused via DCOM (e.g., excel.exe, wmiprvse.exe)
Known set of systems that should or should not be invoking DCOM activity

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to log into remote machines using Secure Shell (SSH). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user. SSH is a protocol that allows authorized users to open remote shells on other computers. Many Linux and macOS versions come with SSH installed by default, although typically disabled until the user enables it. On ESXi, SSH can be enabled either directly on the host (e.

description.en: SSH login from a remote system (via sshd), followed by user context execution of suspicious binaries or privilege escalation behavior.

mutableElements.description: Defines correlation window from login to first post-SSH process (e.g., 60s)
List of binaries considered unusual in SSH context (e.g., nc, base64, bash -i)
Accounts of interest for SSH logins (e.g., root, admin)

description.en: SSH login detected via Unified Logs, followed by unusual process execution, especially outside normal user behavior patterns.

mutableElements.description: Time range to correlate post-SSH activities (e.g., 45s)
Define authorized users to reduce false positives
Suspicious terms like reverse shells, base64, curl

description.en: SSH login via hostd or /var/log/auth.log, followed by CLI access to host shell or file manipulation in restricted areas.

mutableElements.description: Legitimate SSH users to this host
Correlate SSH login and unauthorized commands or shell access
Flag commands like esxcli, rm, chmod post-login

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to remotely control machines using Virtual Network Computing (VNC). VNC is a platform-independent desktop sharing system that uses the RFB (“remote framebuffer”) protocol to enable users to remotely control another computer’s display by relaying the screen, mouse, and keyboard inputs over the network.

description.en: Detection of VNC service or executable starting unexpectedly, followed by user session creation and interactive desktop activity (mouse/keyboard simulation).

mutableElements.description: Correlate VNC process with user logon activity within defined time span
Trackable VNC executable names (e.g., vncserver.exe, winvnc.exe)
Limit detection to interactive logons (type 10)

description.en: Spawning of VNC-related processes (e.g., x11vnc, vncserver) coupled with authentication logs and port listening behavior on TCP 5900.

mutableElements.description: Default VNC port (5900) but may vary in config
Filter specific VNC binaries in process execution logs
Scope detection to non-service or high-privilege accounts

description.en: Detection of VNC-based remote control via screensharingd activity in Unified Logs along with concurrent remote login activity or suspicious user interaction.

mutableElements.description: Unified log predicate to refine suspicious screensharing access
Time between VNC connection and follow-on activity (e.g., 30s)
Mouse/keyboard interaction spike immediately post-VNC login

brief.en: Adversaries may use Valid Accounts to interact with remote systems using Windows Remote Management (WinRM). The adversary may then perform actions as the logged-on user. WinRM is the name of both a Windows service and a protocol that allows a user to interact with a remote system (e.g., run an executable, modify the Registry, modify services).

description.en: Adversaries using WinRM to remotely execute commands, launch child processes, or access WMI. The detection chain includes service use, network activity, remote session logon, and process creation within a short temporal window.

mutableElements.description: Defines max time between remote shell creation and child process execution (e.g., 60 seconds)
Scope to unexpected remote user logons (non-admins, service accounts)
Score for suspicious command usage via WinRM (e.g., encoded PowerShell)
List of trusted systems allowed to use WinRM legitimately

brief.en: Adversaries may log into accessible cloud services within a compromised environment using Valid Accounts that are synchronized with or federated to on-premises user identities. The adversary may then perform management actions or access cloud-hosted resources as the logged-on user.

description.en: Cloud login from atypical geolocation or user-agent string, followed by resource enumeration or infrastructure manipulation using cloud CLI/API

mutableElements.description: Tunable scoring system for evaluating geo-divergent or TOR-origin logins
Flag rare CLI tools or browser-based sessions
Threshold for how long between login and API access
Limit monitoring to high-value resource groups or sensitive tenants

description.en: Federated login using SSO or OAuth grant to cloud control plane, followed by directory or permissions enumeration

mutableElements.description: Tune based on applications federated to high-priv cloud assets
Filter based on expected OIDC clients used for login
Track multiple geographic logins within short windows

description.en: Login to M365 or Google Workspace from CLI tools or unexpected source IPs, followed by mailbox or document access

mutableElements.description: Raise alerts on login from CLI when user typically uses web-only
Track access to documents labeled as internal/confidential
Tune for high-volume document reads post login

description.en: Remote access to third-party SaaS with OAuth or API tokens post-initial compromise, followed by sensitive data access or configuration changes

mutableElements.description: Older tokens issued before password change may indicate compromise
Restrict detection to high-value or regulated SaaS apps

brief.en: Adversaries may leverage Valid Accounts to log directly into accessible cloud hosted compute infrastructure through cloud native methods. Many cloud providers offer interactive connections to virtual infrastructure that can be accessed through the Cloud API, such as Azure Serial Console, AWS EC2 Instance Connect, and AWS System Manager..

description.en: Direct login to cloud-hosted virtual machines via cloud-native access methods (e.g., EC2 Instance Connect, Azure Serial Console, SSM), followed by command execution or privilege escalation on the VM

mutableElements.description: Correlates cloud login to host activity within a reasonable time span (e.g., < 60 seconds)
Filters based on access vector: SSH key, SSM session, or Console connect
Identifies sessions from out-of-region or untrusted networks
Filters sensitive systems or production assets for alert tuning

brief.en: Adversaries may search connected removable media on computers they have compromised to find files of interest. Sensitive data can be collected from any removable media (optical disk drive, USB memory, etc.) connected to the compromised system prior to Exfiltration. Interactive command shells may be in use, and common functionality within cmd may be used to gather information.

description.en: Adversary mounts a USB device and begins enumerating, copying, or compressing files using scripting engines, cmd, or remote access tools.

mutableElements.description: Can tune based on known removable device labels or whitelist
Controls timing between device mount and sensitive file access
Tune for sensitive file extensions (e.g., .docx, .pdf, .csv)

description.en: Adversary mounts external drive to /media or /mnt then accesses or copies targeted data via shell, cp, or tar.

mutableElements.description: Filter for unexpected or user-defined mount locations (e.g., /media/usb)
Tune based on read/write access types seen during collection

description.en: Adversary attaches USB drive and accesses sensitive files using Finder, cp, or bash scripts.

mutableElements.description: Tune by filtering removable media mounted under /Volumes
Correlate activity to admin or service accounts for priority

brief.en: Adversaries may use binary padding to add junk data and change the on-disk representation of malware. This can be done without affecting the functionality or behavior of a binary, but can increase the size of the binary beyond what some security tools are capable of handling due to file size limitations.

description.en: Detects the creation or execution of padded binary files (e.g., large size but minimal legitimate content) followed by process execution or lateral movement from the host.

mutableElements.description: Threshold size in MB to determine suspicious padding
Correlation time window between file creation and execution
Scope the detection to suspicious or non-standard user accounts

description.en: Detects abnormal creation of binary files with significant size that are subsequently executed or accessed by non-standard users.

mutableElements.description: Defines how large a file must be to consider it padded
Target abnormal user behavior outside of expected automation
Time window for correlating file creation and execution

description.en: Monitors for anomalous binary files written to disk with padded size and subsequent execution by user or service context.

mutableElements.description: Padded binary threshold for file size
Detection correlation window for execution after file creation
Filters for specific users or groups such as admin or service accounts

brief.en: Adversaries may perform software packing or virtual machine software protection to conceal their code. Software packing is a method of compressing or encrypting an executable. Packing an executable changes the file signature in an attempt to avoid signature-based detection. Most decompression techniques decompress the executable code in memory.

description.en: Detection of unpacking behavior through abnormal memory allocation, followed by executable code injection and execution from non-image sections.

mutableElements.description: To scope detections to suspicious parent-child process relationships typical of loaders or droppers.
To tune for unusually large virtual memory allocations that might indicate unpacked payloads.

description.en: Correlates ELF file execution with high-entropy writable memory segments and self-modifying code patterns.

mutableElements.description: Useful for tuning unpacked sections containing high entropy indicative of compression or encryption.
Can be tuned to correlate file writes to execution within a set timeframe.

description.en: Detection of packed Mach-O binaries unpacking into memory and transferring control to dynamically modified code segments.

mutableElements.description: Helps to distinguish between signed/unsigned packed binaries (common in legitimate vs. malicious cases).
Can be used to scope to specific users or service accounts targeted in attacks.

brief.en: Adversaries may use steganography techniques in order to prevent the detection of hidden information. Steganographic techniques can be used to hide data in digital media such as images, audio tracks, video clips, or text files. Duqu was an early example of malware that used steganography.

description.en: Detects execution of image viewers or PowerShell scripts accessing or decoding files with mismatched MIME headers or embedded script-like byte patterns; often correlated with suspicious parent-child process lineage and outbound connections.

mutableElements.description: Tune to identify image editors/viewers invoking script interpreters (e.g., mspaint.exe > powershell.exe)
Adjust tolerance for image file headers that do not match file extensions or content structure
Define the temporal range to correlate decoding → execution → network beaconing

description.en: Detects access to media files followed by execution of scripts (bash, Python, etc.) referencing those same files, or outbound traffic triggered shortly after file read. Correlates unusual use of tools like steghide, exiftool, or image libraries.

mutableElements.description: Define the list of steganographic or image-parsing tools to alert on (e.g., steghide, imagemagick)
Tune to detect script engines accessing media files (e.g., python script.py image.png)

description.en: Detects manipulation of PNG, JPG, or GIF files by user-initiated scripts followed by script execution or exfiltration behavior, especially from osascript, python, or bash, in combination with LaunchAgent persistence or curl activity.

mutableElements.description: Adapt to known or emerging tools using stego methods on macOS (e.g., Invoke-PSImage, stegsolve)
Update list of trusted versus unknown scripting hosts launching activity tied to image handling

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to make payloads difficult to discover and analyze by delivering files to victims as uncompiled code. Text-based source code files may subvert analysis and scrutiny from protections targeting executables/binaries. These payloads will need to be compiled before execution; typically via native utilities such as ilasm.exe, csc.exe, or GCC/MinGW.

description.en: Detects compilation activity using csc.exe, ilasm.exe, or msbuild.exe initiated by user-space processes outside typical development environments, followed by execution or network activity from newly written binaries.

mutableElements.description: Filter for unexpected users (non-dev) launching compilers like csc.exe or msbuild.exe
Adjust paths for sensitive file write zones (e.g., C:\Users\Public\, %TEMP%, or Desktop)
Tune the correlation window between compilation and subsequent execution or C2

description.en: Detects GCC or Clang invoked on suspicious file paths (e.g., /tmp/, ~/Downloads) with output to executable binaries, followed by execution or outbound traffic from these binaries.

mutableElements.description: Specify path and binaries for detection (e.g., /usr/bin/gcc, /opt/mingw/bin/gcc)
Match uncommon chmod behavior post-compilation (e.g., +x in /tmp or home directories)

description.en: Detects non-standard compilation activity via Xcode CLI tools or bundled GCC/MONO packages writing new executable files and executing them outside dev environments (e.g., user Downloads folder).

mutableElements.description: Detect calls to xcodebuild, clang, or /Applications/Mono.app/... from non-admin users
Monitor for output files in user-writable paths (e.g., ~/Library/Caches, ~/Downloads)

brief.en: Adversaries may remove indicators from tools if they believe their malicious tool was detected, quarantined, or otherwise curtailed. They can modify the tool by removing the indicator and using the updated version that is no longer detected by the target's defensive systems or subsequent targets that may use similar systems.

description.en: Detection of known tools or malware flagged by antivirus, followed by a near-term drop of a similar binary with modified signature and resumed activity (execution, C2, or persistence).

mutableElements.description: Vendor-specific signature string or detection message that can be correlated to threat intel context.
The time between AV alert and similar file/process activity (e.g., 5–30 minutes)
String or hash similarity thresholds between original and modified binary.

description.en: Detection of anti-malware quarantining or flagging a tool, followed by a new binary written to disk with a similar function or name and a resumed process chain.

mutableElements.description: Tunable list of directories often abused for dropped binaries (e.g., /tmp, ~/.cache, /opt/soft/).
Limit how far up the tree to trace tool modification behavior for detection.

description.en: Detection of XProtect or AV quarantining a known tool, followed by modification (file size, hash, string) and subsequent re-execution by the same or related user.

mutableElements.description: File hash delta or binary string diff score to tolerate renamed/mutated variants.
User or group expected to use dev tools; reduce false positives from legitimate repacking.

brief.en: Adversaries may smuggle data and files past content filters by hiding malicious payloads inside of seemingly benign HTML files. HTML documents can store large binary objects known as JavaScript Blobs (immutable data that represents raw bytes) that can later be constructed into file-like objects. Data may also be stored in Data URLs, which enable embedding media type or MIME files inline of HTML documents.

description.en: Detection of browser-based or email client-driven file creation (often from temp directories) following navigation to or execution of HTML files containing JavaScript Blob APIs or base64 Data URLs, with follow-on execution of the dropped payload. Leveraging Sysmon EventID 15 to inspect Zone.Identifier ADS for HostUrl/ReferrerUrl indicators (e.g., HostUrl=about:internet). Optional: absence of a large HTTP download record for the same URL/client in proxy logs (suggests local assembly)

mutableElements.description: Time range between HTML file open and file drop + execution (e.g., 1–10 minutes)
Tunable list of file extensions of interest (e.g., .js, .hta, .exe)
Expected processes that may drop files (e.g., browser, Outlook); tune for normal behavior

description.en: Detection of browser-based downloads from HTML sources that trigger file creation in temp or user directories followed by execution of new files within short timeframes and suspicious parent-child lineage.

mutableElements.description: Regular expressions for common download paths (e.g., /tmp/, ~/Downloads/)
Tunable range for follow-up process execution from dropped file (e.g., 5–15 minutes)

description.en: Detection of HTML-based downloads via Safari/Chrome that create obfuscated files (e.g., .zip, .app, .js) in user directories and are followed by suspicious executions from preview or launch services.

mutableElements.description: Whether downloaded file has a quarantine flag and is bypassed via Gatekeeper
JavaScript strings that may indicate smuggling: msSaveBlob, download.href, createObjectURL

brief.en: Adversaries may obfuscate then dynamically resolve API functions called by their malware in order to conceal malicious functionalities and impair defensive analysis. Malware commonly uses various Native API functions provided by the OS to perform various tasks such as those involving processes, files, and other system artifacts.

description.en: Behavioral chain involving suspicious use of GetProcAddress and LoadLibrary following memory allocation and manual mapping, often paired with low entropy strings, abnormal API use without static import tables, or delayed module load behaviors.

logSources.name: etw:Microsoft-Windows-Kernel-Process
logSources.channel: API tracing / stack tracing via ETW or telemetry-based EDR

mutableElements.description: Tunable logic to flag suspicious modules used without static IAT entries
Correlates module load to suspicious memory allocation or API lookup within timeframe
Used to detect obfuscated strings or hashed function names
Optional filtering of known safe modules or patterns from telemetry

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to make a payload difficult to analyze by removing symbols, strings, and other human readable information. Scripts and executables may contain variables names and other strings that help developers document code functionality. Symbols are often created by an operating system’s linker when executable payloads are compiled.

description.en: Executable or script payloads lacking symbol information and readable strings that are created or dropped by unusual or short-lived processes.

logSources.channel: File Metadata Inspection (Low String Entropy, Missing PDB)

mutableElements.description: Payloads with extremely low string entropy may indicate stripped or obfuscated binaries
Used to scope or whitelist common system builders, compilers, or admin tools
Correlates file creation and process spawning within a short timeframe

description.en: Executable or binary files created without symbol tables or with stripped sections, especially by non-user shell processes or compilers invoked outside standard dev paths.

mutableElements.description: Flag combinations in compiled binaries indicating symbol table removal
Whitelist compiler output directories to reduce false positives
Heuristic boundaries for abnormal small or overly large stripped binaries

description.en: Creation of run-only AppleScripts or Mach-O binaries lacking symbol table and string references, especially when dropped by user space scripting engines or staging apps.

mutableElements.description: AppleScript flag to disable reverse engineering (run-only compiled scripts)
Filter to isolate staging or suspicious scripting engines
Tuning based on unsigned vs. developer-signed payloads

description.en: Inbound binary payloads transferred over HTTP/S with compressed or encoded headers, lacking signature markers or metadata indicative of compiler/toolchain.

mutableElements.description: Tune for octet-stream or mismatched Content-Type headers
Payload threshold for executable-sized artifacts
Suspicious base64 or chunked encoding not matching normal app behavior

brief.en: Adversaries may embed payloads within other files to conceal malicious content from defenses. Otherwise seemingly benign files (such as scripts and executables) may be abused to carry and obfuscate malicious payloads and content. In some cases, embedded payloads may also enable adversaries to Subvert Trust Controls by not impacting execution controls such as digital signatures and notarization tickets.

description.en: Detection of executables or scripts containing hidden embedded resources or secondary payloads, often with anomalies in file size vs. functionality or dropped child binaries.

mutableElements.description: Threshold in bytes where appended sections to binaries are considered suspicious
Controls how far child process lineage is analyzed for dropped embedded payloads
Defines correlation interval between file write and process execution

description.en: Detection of shell scripts, ELF binaries, or archives containing embedded secondary payloads, self-extracting components, or unusual compression behavior during runtime.

mutableElements.description: Tuning value for ELF binaries with appended sections or resources
Threshold for long shell scripts with base64-encoded binary content
Number of files written from a single script execution

description.en: Detection of Mach-O binaries or AppleScripts that contain nested, encoded, or run-only embedded payloads dropped at runtime.

mutableElements.description: Run-only AppleScripts or signed scripting payloads may require scoped detection
Threshold on number of binaries created by the parent payload
Allows focusing on suspicious interpreter or staging tools

brief.en: Adversaries may obfuscate content during command execution to impede detection. Command-line obfuscation is a method of making strings and patterns within commands and scripts more difficult to signature and analyze. This type of obfuscation can be included within commands executed by delivered payloads (e.g., Phishing and Drive-by Compromise) or interactively via Command and Scripting Interpreter.

description.en: Detection of command-line activity exhibiting syntactic obfuscation patterns, such as excessive escape characters, base64 encoding, command concatenation, or outlier command length and entropy.

mutableElements.description: Used to flag base64 or token-heavy command-line strings
Escape character and symbol frequency in command-line strings
Window between command execution and follow-up child or file write behavior

description.en: Detection of shell commands that leverage encoded execution, command chaining, excessive piping, or unusual token patterns indicative of obfuscation.

mutableElements.description: Tuning value for token or argument count in shell invocations
Environment-specific regex patterns for encoded or eval'd command lines
Shell-specific globbing or directory traversal string detection

description.en: Detection of obfuscated commands via shell, osascript, or AppleScript interpreters using unusual tokens, encoding, variable substitution, or runtime string reconstruction.

mutableElements.description: Limits detection scope to shell or scripting interpreters like zsh, bash, osascript
Minimum entropy required to consider the command or script obfuscated
Deviation from baseline for long or highly nested arguments

brief.en: Adversaries may store data in "fileless" formats to conceal malicious activity from defenses. Fileless storage can be broadly defined as any format other than a file. Common examples of non-volatile fileless storage in Windows systems include the Windows Registry, event logs, or WMI repository.

description.en: Detects abuse of fileless storage mechanisms such as Registry keys, WMI classes, and Event Logs used to stage payloads, scripts, or encoded content outside traditional files.

mutableElements.description: Scoped to suspicious or abused paths like HKCU\Software\Classes\ or HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\
Minimum entropy level to flag suspicious registry or WMI content as encoded payloads
Temporal window for correlating WMI/registry modifications with process creation or network usage

description.en: Detects usage of shared memory directories (/dev/shm, /run/shm) for temporary storage of obfuscated, encoded, or executable data without persistence to disk.

mutableElements.description: Shared memory mount path used (e.g., /dev/shm/ or /run/shm/)
Regex to match non-standard, suspicious, or encoded filenames
Time window to correlate process execution from shared memory directories

brief.en: Adversaries may smuggle commands to download malicious payloads past content filters by hiding them within otherwise seemingly benign windows shortcut files. Windows shortcut files (.LNK) include many metadata fields, including an icon location field (also known as the IconEnvironmentDataBlock) designed to specify the path to an icon file that is to be displayed for the LNK file within a host directory.

description.en: Correlates LNK file execution with embedded resource extraction or suspicious network activity following initial launch, often leading to payload delivery via disguised icons.

mutableElements.description: Can be tuned to focus on common launcher processes like explorer.exe or winword.exe.

Could be used to focus on .lnk files only or track associated dropped payloads like .dat, .exe, etc.

brief.en: Adversaries may encrypt or encode files to obfuscate strings, bytes, and other specific patterns to impede detection. Encrypting and/or encoding file content aims to conceal malicious artifacts within a file used in an intrusion. Many other techniques, such as Software Packing, Steganography, and Embedded Payloads, share this same broad objective.

description.en: Detection of processes that load or decode encrypted/encoded files in memory and subsequently execute or inject them, indicating payload unpacking or memory-resident malware.

mutableElements.description: Path of decoder utilities (e.g., certutil.exe, powershell.exe) can vary across environments.
Base64/hex strings used may change per encoded payload.
The duration between file decode and execution may differ across implementations.

description.en: Detection of suspicious use of shell utilities or scripts that decode or decrypt a payload and execute it without writing to disk.

mutableElements.description: Normal usage of base64, openssl, or gpg varies by user/role.
Parent-child process chains may differ across deployments.
Time between decode and execution is implementation-specific.

description.en: Detection of encoded payloads being decoded and executed in-memory using scripting tools or third-party decoders.

mutableElements.description: Encoded payload content varies across adversaries.

brief.en: Adversaries may utilize polymorphic code (also known as metamorphic or mutating code) to evade detection. Polymorphic code is a type of software capable of changing its runtime footprint during code execution. With each execution of the software, the code is mutated into a different version of itself that achieves the same purpose or objective as the original.

description.en: Identifies self-modifying executables that exhibit changes in binary hash, entropy, or memory sections during or between executions—often tied to dynamic unpacking or decryption behaviors.

mutableElements.description: Tune based on expected baseline entropy for executables; higher values may indicate polymorphic packing.
Correlate rapid process spawn + image load activity suggesting mutation engine usage.
Define expected or suspicious parent-child chains (e.g., script runner -> encoded PE)

description.en: Detects files or processes where execution results in frequent re-creation or modification of ELF binaries or interpreter scripts, often using chmod + execve with abnormal entropy.

mutableElements.description: Tune to alert on write followed by chmod + exec in quick succession.
Detect high deviation from average entropy score of baseline ELF/script files.
Abnormal burst executions of file with identical functionality but varying hash.

description.en: Tracks modification of executables or interpreter payloads (e.g., Mach-O, dylib) that mutate across runs—using scripting engines, JIT compilers, or side-loaded plugins.

mutableElements.description: Detection may vary based on whether Python/Swift/AppleScript is used to mutate payloads.
Entropy tuning based on expected baseline for system vs user binaries.
Helps flag apps that change but maintain signed status across invocations.

brief.en: Adversaries may use compression to obfuscate their payloads or files. Compressed file formats such as ZIP, gzip, 7z, and RAR can compress and archive multiple files together to make it easier and faster to transfer files. In addition to compressing files, adversaries may also compress shellcode directly - for example, in order to store it in a Windows Registry key (i.e., Fileless Storage).

description.en: Monitors for compression tool usage (e.g., 7zip, WinRAR, MakeCab) that follows or precedes file modification, suspicious file types (e.g., .exe, .dll) being compressed, or dropped from self-extracting archives followed by immediate execution.

mutableElements.description: Zip, .rar, .cab, .gz – tune based on expected legitimate use of compression in environment
