mutableElements.description: Legitimate system processes that may rarely spawn network-capable child processes (e.g., rundll32, svchost).
Watch for high-numbered ports or well-known proxy ports like 1080, 8080, 4444.
Capture unusual spikes in outbound connections over a short period.

description.en: User-space tools (e.g., socat, ncat, iptables, ssh) used in non-standard ways to establish reverse shells, port-forwarding, or inter-host connections. Often chained with uncommon outbound destinations or SSH tunnels.

mutableElements.description: Shell piping into tools like socat, ncat, or openssl for tunnel creation.
Flag connections made from internal systems to uncommon high ports externally.
Capture low-privilege or unexpected users executing system-level network tools.

description.en: AppleScript, LaunchAgents, or remote login services (ssh, networksetup) establishing proxy tunnels or dynamic port forwards to external IPs or alternate local hosts.

mutableElements.description: Identify suspicious domains often associated with CDN-routed or anonymized endpoints (e.g., Cloudflare, Fastly).
Alert when AppleScript or Automator tools are used for network tunneling tasks.
Monitor for LaunchAgents executing proxy tools or dynamic ports.

description.en: Direct use of nc, socat, or reverse tunnel scripts initiated by abnormal user contexts or unauthorized VIBs initiating connections from hypervisor to external systems.

mutableElements.description: Custom proxy or port forwarding scripts executed from ESXi shell.
Unusual outbound connections from ESXi host, particularly to internet.
Root or elevated users initiating unexpected tunnels.

description.en: Dynamic or static port forwarding rules added to route traffic through an internal host, or configuration changes to proxy firewall rules not aligned with baselined policy.

mutableElements.description: Focus on new allow/permit rules with dynamic NAT or port forwarders.
Flag any non-admins initiating proxy config changes.
Detect sharp changes in bi-directional traffic patterns.

brief.en: Adversaries may use an internal proxy to direct command and control traffic between two or more systems in a compromised environment. Many tools exist that enable traffic redirection through proxies or port redirection, including HTRAN, ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap.

description.en: Anomalous process (e.g., rundll32, svchost, cmd) initiates connections to internal peer hosts not seen in typical communication baselines, used to proxy or forward traffic internally, often using SMB, RPC, or high ports.

mutableElements.description: Tune based on known host-to-host communications that are rare (e.g., workstation-to-workstation).
Focus on unusual internal traffic on ports like 1080, 8080, 4444, or SMB over non-standard ports.
Correlate unusual traffic bursts with new process execution.

description.en: socat, ssh, iptables, or ncat invoked from user space or cron jobs to create port forwarding, reverse shells, or inter-host tunnels between compromised Linux systems. Behavior is typically paired with socket activity and high entropy traffic.

mutableElements.description: Alert on unexpected users executing inter-host relay tools (e.g., www-data, backup).
Adjust to watch for commonly misused internal TCP/UDP ports.
Shell pipelines or wrapped invocations like bash -c 'socat ...'

description.en: Execution of AppleScript or Automator services launching ssh -L, socat, or launchctl items that dynamically reroute traffic from one Mac endpoint to another. LaunchAgents used to establish permanent internal tunnels.

mutableElements.description: Directory where proxying LaunchDaemons may be dropped, e.g., /Library/LaunchDaemons/.
Dynamic port forwards often use ephemeral or non-standard service ports.
May trigger on less common scripting interfaces for traffic redirection.

description.en: ESXi shell execution of tools/scripts (nc, socat, perl) relaying network traffic to other internal hosts, especially when initiated by unauthorized users or VMs.

mutableElements.description: Watch for chained shell commands building local-to-local connections.
Correlate to which VM initiated the traffic tunnel; unexpected VM behavior may be suspicious.
Unusual east-west communication patterns among VMs.

description.en: Configuration of internal NAT or proxy rules that redirect traffic between client segments internally (e.g., site-to-site port forwarding). Often used to relay internal beaconing or move traffic laterally through trust zones.

mutableElements.description: Internal subnets or endpoint roles allowed for port forwarding.
Detect changes made outside scheduled or authorized windows.
Volume of data relayed through proxy exceeds historical norms.

brief.en: Adversaries may use an external proxy to act as an intermediary for network communications to a command and control server to avoid direct connections to their infrastructure. Many tools exist that enable traffic redirection through proxies or port redirection, including HTRAN, ZXProxy, and ZXPortMap.

description.en: Unusual process (e.g., rundll32, mshta, wscript, or custom payloads) initiates network connection to external IPs/domains that proxy C2 traffic, often over uncommon ports or high entropy HTTP/S connections.

mutableElements.description: Adjust for known benign but high-risk infrastructure (e.g., hosting providers like DigitalOcean, OVH, etc.).
Detect suspicious lineage—proxy tools launched from script interpreters or LOLBins.
Tune based on expected randomness in outbound request payloads.

description.en: curl, wget, ncat, socat, or custom binaries initiate outbound traffic to Internet-based proxies (e.g., via VPS or CDN). Behavior may include reverse shell constructs or persistent outbound beacons.

mutableElements.description: Regex or command substring matches indicative of dynamic proxy setup.
Tunable list of IPs or ASNs related to known proxy/VPS abuse.
Unexpected users running networking tools (e.g., www-data, apache).

description.en: AppleScript or terminal sessions launch tools (curl, nc, ssh) to external IPs not commonly accessed. Outbound connections are made by LaunchAgents/LaunchDaemons, often masquerading as system services.

mutableElements.description: Detect persistence used to restart proxy after reboot.
Often high or non-standard ports, configurable for outbound proxy detection.
Flag unsigned or anomalous binaries making external connections.

description.en: ESXi shell or guest VM tools initiate external connections via scripted traffic forwarding to Internet-based proxies. Detected by firewall or shell audit logs showing outbound connection spikes from hypervisor or guest VM to remote proxy nodes.

mutableElements.description: Detect when VMs communicate with Internet IPs not in workload profiles.
Regex for proxy-related tools/scripts executed on the host.
Outbound only connections from ESXi to new IPs.

description.en: Changes to NAT/firewall policies enabling outbound port forwarding from internal IPs to Internet-based proxy endpoints. Log spikes in outbound flows to CDN, VPS, or anomalous ASNs with few return packets.

mutableElements.description: Number of flows or bytes transferred per minute—flag surges to unrecognized ASNs.
Proxy destination categories: CDN, TOR exit node, anonymous hosting.
Track if unexpected user or automation changed NAT/forwarding rules.

brief.en: Adversaries may chain together multiple proxies to disguise the source of malicious traffic. Typically, a defender will be able to identify the last proxy traffic traversed before it enters their network; the defender may or may not be able to identify any previous proxies before the last-hop proxy.

description.en: Suspicious processes (e.g., Tor clients, relays, unknown binaries) launch with sustained encrypted outbound traffic to known anonymity infrastructure (e.g., Tor, I2P), and may relay to additional internal systems via reverse proxying, ICMP tunneling, or socket forwarding.

logSources.name: dns:query
logSources.channel: Outbound resolution to hidden service domains (e.g., `.onion`)

mutableElements.description: Can be tuned to .onion, I2P, or suspicious CDN domains.
Detect known-good vs. abnormal launching binaries (e.g., mshta spawning Tor).
Threshold for persistent connections over known relay ports (e.g., 9050).

description.en: Tools such as tor, nglite, proxychains, chisel, or custom daemons repeatedly initiate outbound sessions to multiple nodes before final destination. This behavior is abnormal for Linux services outside of VPN, monitoring, or CDN relay contexts.

mutableElements.description: Match known proxy tools, tuned for environment.
Detect outbound chaining behavior through >2 IPs in short succession.
Allow filtering by ICMP, TCP/443, UDP for obfuscation channels.

description.en: LaunchAgents or LaunchDaemons initiate persistent Tor or relay processes that make encrypted outbound connections. May be paired with sandbox bypasses or unsigned executables communicating over SOCKS proxies.

mutableElements.description: Regex for masking patterns in LaunchAgents with proxy behavior.
Allow for exceptions for known unsigned binaries.
Monitor local 9050/9150 activity and rerouted system traffic.

description.en: Outbound encrypted traffic initiated from hypervisor shell or via VM backdoor mechanisms to relays in VPS infrastructure, especially if traversing multiple nodes before reaching Internet destination. Packet captures or firewall logs show non-VM communication paths.

mutableElements.description: Threshold on number of IPs contacted in sequence without DNS resolution.
Flag if relay communication initiated by ESXi shell or unknown VM agent.
Filter for known Tor/VPS egress networks.

description.en: Encrypted traffic or ICMP tunneling from border routers to internal routers or unknown external IPs. Forwarded traffic shows consistent hop-to-hop relaying without matching configured VPN or expected network topology.

mutableElements.description: Define allowed internal router communication paths.
High entropy ICMP payloads may indicate tunneling activity.
Track known multi-hop pattern signatures or port hopping techniques.

brief.en: Adversaries may take advantage of routing schemes in Content Delivery Networks (CDNs) and other services which host multiple domains to obfuscate the intended destination of HTTPS traffic or traffic tunneled through HTTPS. Domain fronting involves using different domain names in the SNI field of the TLS header and the Host field of the HTTP header.

description.en: Suspicious outbound HTTPS connections where the TLS Server Name Indication (SNI) does not match the HTTP Host header, indicating potential use of domain fronting to mask C2 traffic via CDNs.

mutableElements.description: Define acceptable mismatch ratio between SNI and HTTP Host fields based on legitimate domain usage patterns.
Whitelist of known safe CDN front-end domains (e.g., cdn.company.com).
Filter for suspicious initiators of domain fronting, e.g., scripting engines, lolbins, unknown binaries.

description.en: Applications such as curl, wget, or custom binaries initiate HTTPS connections where the TLS SNI is mismatched or absent while HTTP Host targets CDN-available C2 endpoints.

mutableElements.description: Detect TLS sessions where SNI is empty—'domainless' fronting.
Environmental tuning for known binaries using alternate SNI for testing (e.g., API tests).
Enrich command-line arguments or parent-child lineage to detect abuse.

description.en: Unsigned or user-space apps initiate TLS connections with one hostname and HTTP headers requesting a different domain, commonly abused in CDN-resident domain fronting techniques.

mutableElements.description: Helps tune detection when unsigned apps initiate fronted sessions.
Threshold to flag inconsistent domain targeting in encrypted sessions.
Alert on unusual ports used in HTTPS+SOCKS activity patterns.

description.en: Traffic originating from ESXi hosts or management interfaces displays SNI-to-Host mismatch behavior, particularly anomalous given typical infrastructure communication patterns.

mutableElements.description: ESXi hosts should rarely initiate external HTTPS—threshold to alert.
Define entropy or timing anomalies for TLS handshake.
SNI/Host mismatch occurrence tolerance.

brief.en: Adversaries may move onto systems, possibly those on disconnected or air-gapped networks, by copying malware to removable media and taking advantage of Autorun features when the media is inserted into a system and executes.

description.en: Execution of files originating from removable media after drive mount, with correlation to file write activity, autorun usage, or lateral spread via staged tools.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Windows Defender/Operational
logSources.channel: Suspicious file execution on removable media path

mutableElements.description: Detect activity on mounted drives typically used by USB (e.g., E:, F:, G:). Tune based on enterprise usage.
Set timing threshold for execution shortly after drive mount (e.g., < 5 minutes).
Restrict detection to suspicious process lineage like explorer.exe, powershell.exe, or unsigned binaries.
Use entropy thresholding to detect packed/obfuscated payloads dropped to removable media.

brief.en: Adversaries can perform command and control between compromised hosts on potentially disconnected networks using removable media to transfer commands from system to system. Both systems would need to be compromised, with the likelihood that an Internet-connected system was compromised first and the second through lateral movement by Replication Through Removable Media.

description.en: Behavioral sequence where removable media is mounted, files are written/updated, and subsequently read/executed on a separate host, suggesting removable-media relay communication.

mutableElements.description: Adjust drive letters used in detection (e.g., E:, F:, G:) depending on enterprise usage.
Tunable window for file write on one host followed by file read or execution on another (e.g., within 10 minutes).
Common naming schemes for payload, tasking, or exfil files (e.g., task.txt, beacon.log, data.bin).

description.en: Detection of file write-access to USB-mount directories (e.g., /media/, /run/media/) followed by same-file access or execution on another host.

mutableElements.description: Typical mount paths to monitor (e.g., /media/usb, /run/media/username/).
Tunable detection window to correlate read/write between different hosts within a short interval (e.g., <15m).

description.en: Correlates removable volume mounts (disk arbitration) with file I/O events on that volume, followed by same file execution shortly after insert.

mutableElements.description: Known suspicious USB volume labels or types (e.g., NO NAME, SECUREDATA).
Unusual processes accessing USB drives (e.g., bash, Python, unsigned binaries).

brief.en: Adversaries may use an OSI non-application layer protocol for communication between host and C2 server or among infected hosts within a network. The list of possible protocols is extensive.

description.en: Anomalous use of ICMP or UDP by non-network service processes for data exfiltration or remote control, especially if traffic bypasses proxy infrastructure or shows unusual flow patterns.

mutableElements.description: Processes normally allowed to use ICMP/UDP (e.g., ping.exe, DNS resolver).
Suspicion if client sends much more data than it receives (e.g., >90%).
Baseline which protocols are normal per host or segment (ICMP, UDP, etc.).

description.en: ICMP or raw socket traffic generated by user-mode processes like bash, Python, or nc, typically using ping, hping3, or crafted packets via libpcap or scapy.

mutableElements.description: Uncommon programs using raw sockets (e.g., netcat, Python, nmap).
Tunable window for correlating execution with network events (e.g., 2m).

description.en: Unsigned binaries or interpreted scripts initiating non-standard protocols (ICMP, UDP, SOCKS) outside of baseline network behavior.

mutableElements.description: Detection threshold for unsigned or transient binaries making ICMP/UDP calls.

description.en: VMCI (Virtual Machine Communication Interface) traffic between guest and host, or between VMs, originating from non-management tools or unauthorized binaries.

mutableElements.description: Monitor for non-vSphere or VMware-native processes using VMCI.
Baseline pattern of guest-to-host traffic vs anomaly (unexpected port, volume).

description.en: Non-standard port/protocol pairings or low-entropy ICMP traffic resembling tunneling patterns (e.g., fixed-size pings with delays).

mutableElements.description: ICMP/UDP packet content entropy filter to identify encoded payloads.
Long ICMP/UDP sessions beyond expected limits (e.g., >5min).

brief.en: Adversaries may add adversary-controlled credentials to a cloud account to maintain persistent access to victim accounts and instances within the environment. For example, adversaries may add credentials for Service Principals and Applications in addition to existing legitimate credentials in Azure / Entra ID. These credentials include both x509 keys and passwords.

description.en: Addition of credentials (keys, app passwords, x.509 certs) to existing cloud accounts, service principals, or OAuth apps via portal or API by non-standard identities or IP ranges.

logSources.name: azure:audit
logSources.channel: Add service principal credentials, app password added, app role assignment

mutableElements.description: App password or legacy auth activity bypassing MFA policies.
Expected IPs allowed to perform admin identity operations.
Track types like clientsecret, certificate, password, federated.

description.en: Cloud API usage to create/import SSH keys or generate new access keys (CreateAccessKey, ImportKeyPair, CreateLoginProfile) from non-console access or unusual principals.

mutableElements.description: Track root, federated identities, and STS tokens separately.
Time between key creation and first use (default: 5 min).
Expected services/accounts allowed to create keys.

description.en: Credential-related configuration changes in productivity apps, such as API key creation in Google Workspace, app tokens in Slack, or user-level OAuth credentials in M365.

logSources.name: gcp:audit
logSources.channel: API Key Created, OAuth Client Registered

mutableElements.description: Detect suspicious redirect URI mismatches in new clients.
Highlight credentials granting excessive read/write org-wide.

brief.en: Adversaries may grant additional permission levels to maintain persistent access to an adversary-controlled email account. For example, the Add-MailboxPermission PowerShell cmdlet, available in on-premises Exchange and in the cloud-based service Office 365, adds permissions to a mailbox.

description.en: Detection of anomalous or unauthorized mailbox delegation activity (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission, Default/Anonymous mailbox permissions, Gmail delegation setup).

mutableElements.description: Threshold for unexpected delegate roles such as FullAccess or SendAs.
Mailbox folder targeted by delegation (Inbox, Root, Calendar, etc.).
Pairings of delegate and delegator users that are expected.
Spike in outbound mail after delegate addition, used to catch phishing or mass exfil.

description.en: Execution of PowerShell commands that modify mailbox permissions using Exchange cmdlets (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission), often tied to BEC or post-compromise persistence.

mutableElements.description: Exchange cmdlets to include or exclude based on scope (e.g., Add-MailboxPermission, Set-MailboxFolderPermission).
Flag suspicious script or interactive shell launch by non-admins.
Window in which Add-MailboxPermission is followed by anomalous usage (e.g., SendAs events).

brief.en: An adversary may add additional roles or permissions to an adversary-controlled cloud account to maintain persistent access to a tenant. For example, adversaries may update IAM policies in cloud-based environments or add a new global administrator in Office 365 environments.

description.en: Detection of new IAM roles or policies attached to a user/service in AWS/GCP/Azure outside normal patterns or hours, often following account compromise.

mutableElements.description: IAM Role type or privilege level assigned (e.g., Admin, Billing, Viewer)
User, service account, or external federated identity context performing the action
How quickly multiple roles or policies are added after initial access
Cross-account roles from outside trusted tenant list

description.en: Behavioral chain of a user being granted elevated privileges or roles in Entra ID or Okta following suspicious login or account creation activity.

logSources.name: m365:audit
logSources.channel: Add member to role, Add app role assignment

mutableElements.description: Number of accounts allowed to hold sensitive roles like Global Admin
Mechanism by which role was added (PowerShell, API, UI)
Expected user-to-role mapping defined by org policy

description.en: Detection of new admin or role assignment actions within Microsoft 365/O365 environments to elevate access for persistence or lateral movement.

mutableElements.description: Admin role type or application role granted
Time between initial login and privilege change
Was the role assignment local or via federated SSO account

brief.en: Adversaries may modify the SSH authorizedkeys file to maintain persistence on a victim host. Linux distributions, macOS, and ESXi hypervisors commonly use key-based authentication to secure the authentication process of SSH sessions for remote management. The authorizedkeys file in SSH specifies the SSH keys that can be used for logging into the user account for which the file is configured.

description.en: Adversary attempts to gain persistence by modifying ~/.ssh/authorizedkeys via shell, text editor, echo or redirected output.

mutableElements.description: Temporal window to correlate file writes and suspicious process launches (e.g., <60s)
Expected user-to-process correlation (e.g., root writing to non-root authorizedkeys)
Custom SSH path or user home variation (e.g., /etc/skel/.ssh/)

description.en: Insertion of public keys into authorizedkeys using bash/zsh or editor tools, correlated with suspicious process ancestry.

mutableElements.description: Track unusual parent process writing to SSH config (e.g., curl -> bash)
Flag whether shell session was interactive (normal) or spawned remotely (potential abuse)

description.en: Abuse of cloud metadata APIs or CLI to push SSH public keys to authorizedkeys of virtual machines.

mutableElements.description: Custom metadata field (e.g., ssh-keys or custom-key)
Was it an admin, service principal, or automation user initiating?
Privilege level of the VM account receiving the key

description.en: Direct modification of /etc/ssh/keys-<user>/authorizedkeys or enabling SSH in sshdconfig to support public key auth.

mutableElements.description: Could be modified SSH path in hypervisor
Whether shell was enabled beforehand via DCUI or API

description.en: Use of command-line like ip ssh pubkey-chain to bind SSH keys to privileged accounts on routers or switches.

mutableElements.description: Was the role allowed to push persistent config changes?
Variations in syntax or log behavior across device OS

brief.en: Adversaries may register a device to an adversary-controlled account. Devices may be registered in a multifactor authentication (MFA) system, which handles authentication to the network, or in a device management system, which handles device access and compliance. MFA systems, such as Duo or Okta, allow users to associate devices with their accounts in order to complete MFA requirements.

description.en: Adversary registers new devices to compromised user accounts to bypass MFA or conditional access policies via Azure Entra ID, Okta, or Duo self-enrollment portals.

logSources.name: azure:audit
logSources.channel: Operation IN ("Add device", "Add registered users to device", "Add registered owner to device")

mutableElements.description: Define expected admin users to exclude known enrollment behavior
Scope internal vs. external device enrollment sources
Adjust for expected hours of legitimate self-enrollment

description.en: Adversary registers a Windows device to Entra ID or bypasses conditional access by adding device via Intune registration pipeline using stolen credentials.

mutableElements.description: Adjust pattern matching logic for unusual or non-corporate device names
Correlate with prior logon location or device usage behavior
Distinguish between MDM vs manual onboarding vs automated scripts

brief.en: An adversary may add additional roles or permissions to an adversary-controlled user or service account to maintain persistent access to a container orchestration system. For example, an adversary with sufficient permissions may create a RoleBinding or a ClusterRoleBinding to bind a Role or ClusterRole to a Kubernetes account.

description.en: Detects assignment of high-privilege roles to user or service accounts via Kubernetes RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding objects, especially outside of CI/CD automation or from unknown IPs.

logSources.name: kubernetes:audit
logSources.channel: create or update events for RoleBinding or ClusterRoleBinding objects

mutableElements.description: Filter expected sources of automated role assignment (e.g., CI/CD tooling)
Scope to privileged roles like cluster-admin, edit, admin
Detect after-hours or irregular-time assignments
Define known service accounts and privileged operators to reduce noise

brief.en: An adversary may add additional local or domain groups to an adversary-controlled account to maintain persistent access to a system or domain. On Windows, accounts may use the net localgroup and net group commands to add existing users to local and domain groups. On Linux, adversaries may use the usermod command for the same purpose.

description.en: Detects unauthorized additions of users or machine accounts to privileged local or domain groups (e.g., Administrators, Remote Desktop Users).

mutableElements.description: Set to detect high-privileged groups like 'Administrators', 'Domain Admins', or 'Remote Desktop Users'
Restrict detections to business hours or approved maintenance windows
Filter out known automated processes or provisioning systems

description.en: Detects unexpected use of usermod, gpasswd, or direct modification of /etc/group to elevate user group membership.

logSources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
logSources.channel: SYSCALL for usermod or /etc/group file modification

mutableElements.description: Focus on 'sudo', 'wheel', or custom high-privilege groups
Account that initiated the change (e.g., service account or unrecognized user)
Detect elevation outside change windows

description.en: Detects use of dseditgroup or dscl to add users to privileged macOS groups (e.g., admin).

logSources.name: macos:unifiedlog
logSources.channel: Process execution or directory service changes

mutableElements.description: Focus on 'admin' or 'com.apple.accessssh'
Detect unknown or transient users making group changes
Detect group modifications at suspicious times

brief.en: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for relaying data to/from a compromised system. Popular websites, cloud services, and social media acting as a mechanism for C2 may give a significant amount of cover due to the likelihood that hosts within a network are already communicating with them prior to a compromise.

description.en: Detects unusual outbound connections to web services from uncommon processes using SSL/TLS, particularly those exhibiting high outbound data volume or persistence.

mutableElements.description: To tune for unexpected or uncommon executables initiating network connections
Volume of outbound data in short time window (e.g., >1MB in <5 min)
Look for connections persisting outside of normal business hours

description.en: Detects command-line tools, agents, or scripts making outbound HTTPS connections to popular web services like Discord, Slack, Dropbox, or Graph API in an unusual context.

mutableElements.description: Unusual parent-child process behavior initiating external comms (e.g., bash > curl)
Destination hostnames (e.g., .dropboxapi.com, .graph.microsoft.com)
Repeated requests at unusual intervals, suggesting beaconing

description.en: Detects user agents or background services making unauthorized or unscheduled web API calls to cloud/web services over HTTPS.

mutableElements.description: Unsigned or user-modified apps communicating with cloud services
Beacon-like pattern of regular outbound communication

description.en: Detects guest VMs or management agents issuing HTTP(S) traffic to external services without a valid patch management or backup justification.

mutableElements.description: Filter to detect only external/public destinations
Exclude known backup or patch automation services

brief.en: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service to host information that points to additional command and control (C2) infrastructure. Adversaries may post content, known as a dead drop resolver, on Web services with embedded (and often obfuscated/encoded) domains or IP addresses. Once infected, victims will reach out to and be redirected by these resolvers.

description.en: Detection of a process or script that accesses a common web service to retrieve content containing obfuscated indicators of a secondary C2 server (dead drop resolver behavior).

mutableElements.description: FQDN or IP for the hosting site of the dead drop (e.g., pastebin.com, twitter.com)
Defines how close in time the suspicious network and process behavior must occur
Filter by user or system accounts to reduce noise

description.en: Detection of a process or script that accesses a common web service to retrieve content containing obfuscated indicators of a secondary C2 server (dead drop resolver behavior).

mutableElements.description: Dead drop hosting domain (e.g., GitHub, Google Docs)
Detects high entropy in payloads signaling obfuscation
Causal proximity between access to resolver and follow-up connections

description.en: Detection of a process or script that accesses a common web service to retrieve content containing obfuscated indicators of a secondary C2 server (dead drop resolver behavior).

mutableElements.description: Known services abused for D2 (e.g., iCloud, Dropbox)
Useful to isolate rare users accessing web services for C2
Max time gap between dead drop resolver fetch and follow-on traffic

description.en: Detection of a process or script that accesses a common web service to retrieve content containing obfuscated indicators of a secondary C2 server (dead drop resolver behavior).

mutableElements.description: Identifies unusual IP destinations embedded in traffic
Used to detect uncommon protocols (e.g., DNS over HTTPS)
Used to correlate outbound web requests with process execution

brief.en: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to and receiving output from a compromised system over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions. Those infected systems can then send the output from those commands back over that Web service channel.

description.en: Suspicious processes initiating encrypted HTTPS connections to common web service domains, followed by abnormal data upload behavior or automated posting behavior indicative of C2 bidirectional traffic.

mutableElements.description: Timeframe for evaluating multiple network connections tied to the same process
Regex or string patterns used to identify common Web service infrastructure (e.g., .googleapis.com)
Minimum data upload size before flagging anomaly
Known benign updaters or service processes to reduce false positives

description.en: Non-interactive system processes making encrypted HTTPS connections to well-known web services followed by high outbound traffic volume or scripted upload patterns.

mutableElements.description: Bias detection toward sessions with larger upload vs download volume
List of known public Web services used for dead drops or C2 (e.g., GitHub, Twitter)
Shell interpreter or automated job parent used for filtering (e.g., /usr/bin/python)

description.en: Scripting engines (e.g., osascript, Python) initiating HTTPS requests to social media or content-sharing platforms, paired with automated response handling indicative of two-way communication.

mutableElements.description: Scripting interpreters to monitor for unusual HTTP traffic (e.g., osascript, ruby, bash)
Patterns or domains used for C2 dead drops and responses (e.g., pastebin.com, twitter.com)
Threshold for number of short-lived HTTPS connections in a short window

brief.en: Adversaries may use an existing, legitimate external Web service as a means for sending commands to a compromised system without receiving return output over the Web service channel. Compromised systems may leverage popular websites and social media to host command and control (C2) instructions.

description.en: Suspicious process initiating outbound connections to web services without corresponding response or return traffic, indicative of one-way command channels.

mutableElements.description: Can tune for popular web services (e.g., googleapis.com, github.com) based on threat actor tooling
May adjust temporal window to catch beaconing patterns (e.g., every 10-30 mins)
Environment-specific tuning to exclude expected update or telemetry tools

description.en: Curl, wget, or custom HTTP clients initiated by uncommon user accounts or cron jobs to popular web services, with no observed response parsing logic.

mutableElements.description: May tune to detect unknown parents like custom scripts or reverse shells
May adjust based on known curl/wget C2 behaviors

description.en: Process using URLSession or similar API to fetch from web services without any response handling, indicative of one-way C2 channels.

mutableElements.description: Flag unexpected outbound activity from non-admin or system users
Optional if script-based obfuscation is seen in web requests

description.en: ESXi shell or scheduled tasks initiating outbound HTTPS to known public services without inbound return or loggable response, used to fetch instructions.

mutableElements.description: Can tune for task names used to execute curl-based outbound requests
Scoped by environment to exclude known legitimate CDNs

brief.en: Adversaries may create multiple stages for command and control that are employed under different conditions or for certain functions. Use of multiple stages may obfuscate the command and control channel to make detection more difficult. Remote access tools will call back to the first-stage command and control server for instructions.

description.en: Initial process initiates outbound connection to first-stage C2, receives payloads or commands, then spawns or injects into a second process that establishes a new outbound connection to an unrelated destination (second-stage C2).

mutableElements.description: Correlate two-stage behavior occurring within a short window (e.g., 1-5 minutes)
Tune to exclude known legitimate updaters and management agents
May be customized to exclude known corporate domains and CDNs

description.en: Shell script or binary initiates curl/wget request to staging domain, writes output to disk or memory, and shortly afterward launches another process that establishes new outbound connection to a different IP or hostname.

mutableElements.description: Tune for suspicious binaries like curl, wget, python, netcat
Detect multiple different external IPs contacted within short timeframe

brief.en: Adversaries may interact with the Windows Registry as part of a variety of other techniques to aid in defense evasion, persistence, and execution. Access to specific areas of the Registry depends on account permissions, with some keys requiring administrator-level access. The built-in Windows command-line utility Reg may be used for local or remote Registry modification.

brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to take screen captures of the desktop to gather information over the course of an operation. Taking a screenshot is also typically possible through native utilities or API calls, such as CopyFromScreen, xwd, or screencapture.

brief.en: Adversaries may target user email to collect sensitive information. Emails may also contain details of ongoing incident response operations, which may allow adversaries to adjust their techniques in order to maintain persistence or evade defenses.

brief.en: Adversaries may target user email on local systems to collect sensitive information. Outlook 2010 and later supports .ost file sizes up to 50GB, while earlier versions of Outlook support up to 20GB.

description.en: Detection focuses on processes that attempt to locate, access, or exfiltrate local Outlook data files (.pst/.ost) using file system access, native Windows utilities (e.g., PowerShell, WMI), or remote access tools with file browsing capabilities. The behavior chain includes directory enumeration, file access, optional compression or staging, and network transfer.

brief.en: Adversaries may target an Exchange server, Office 365, or Google Workspace to collect sensitive information. Adversaries may leverage a user's credentials and interact directly with the Exchange server to acquire information from within a network. Adversaries may also access externally facing Exchange services, Office 365, or Google Workspace to access email using credentials or access tokens.

description.en: Detects adversaries accessing remote mail systems (e.g., Exchange Online, O365) using stolen credentials or OAuth tokens, followed by scripted access to mailbox contents via PowerShell, AADInternals, or unattended API queries. Detection focuses on abnormal logon sessions, user agents, IP locations, and scripted or tool-based email data access.

description.en: CLI tools (smbclient -L, smbmap, rpcclient, nmblookup) or custom scripts enumerate SMB shares on many internal hosts → corresponding SMB connections (445/139) captured by Zeek/Netflow within a short window.

logSources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
logSources.channel: execve of smbclient, smbmap, rpcclient, nmblookup, crackmapexec smb

logSources.channel: connection: TCP connections to ports 139/445 to multiple hosts

logSources.name: NSM:Flow

mutableElements.description: Minimum unique hosts to flag (e.g., ≥5).
Correlation window between tool exec and SMB fan-out (default 10m).
IPs of vulnerability scanners or config mgmt systems.

logSources.channel: Command line contains smbutil view //, mount_smbfs //

Correlation window between exec and SMB connections (default 10m).
Jamf/IT scripts legitimately running smbutil/mountsmbfs.

brief.en: Adversaries may create an account to maintain access to victim systems. With a sufficient level of access, creating such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that do not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system. Accounts may be created on the local system or within a domain or cloud tenant.

description.en: Adversary uses built-in OS tools or API calls to create local or domain accounts for persistence or lateral movement. Tools such as 'net user', PowerShell, or MMC snap-ins may be used. Detection focuses on Event ID 4720 paired with process lineage and user context.

mutableElements.description: Correlation between Event ID 4720 and creating process may vary by environment and automation delays
Tools like net.exe or powershell.exe can be normal or malicious depending on user context
System vs. administrator vs. low-privilege user context changes alert criticality

description.en: Adversary invokes 'useradd', 'adduser', or equivalent system commands or scripts to create local users. Detection focuses on command execution and audit trail of passwd/shadow file modifications.

mutableElements.description: Custom scripts or renamed binaries may evade simple path-based detection
Account creation outside maintenance windows may indicate compromise

description.en: Adversary creates new users using 'dscl' commands, GUI tools, or by modifying user plist files. Detection includes monitoring dscl invocation and user-related plist changes.

mutableElements.description: Attackers may use service-like names to hide malicious accounts
Accounts created via Terminal vs GUI vs remote session can affect confidence

description.en: Adversary creates users via IAM/IdP API or portal (e.g., Azure AD, Okta). Detection involves monitoring API calls, admin action logs, and correlation with role assignments.

mutableElements.description: Trigger alert only when account is assigned privileged roles
Exclude accounts from known automation processes or provisioning pipelines

description.en: Account creation via cloud service APIs or CLI, often associated with key generation. Monitored via CloudTrail or equivalent audit logs.

mutableElements.description: Alert on account creation outside expected geographies
Filter on creation of users scoped to sensitive services

brief.en: Adversaries may create a local account to maintain access to victim systems. Local accounts are those configured by an organization for use by users, remote support, services, or for administration on a single system or service. For example, with a sufficient level of access, the Windows net user /add command can be used to create a local account.

description.en: Adversary uses built-in tools like 'net user /add', PowerShell, or WMI to create a local user. Sequence: Account creation event (4720) follows process creation of a suspicious executable (e.g., powershell.exe or net.exe).

mutableElements.description: Attackers may use cmd.exe, wscript.exe, or renamed binaries to evade detection
Define time threshold between process start and user creation event (e.g., 5s–2m)
Correlate if process runs under SYSTEM, Administrator, or untrusted account

description.en: Local user accounts are created via binaries like 'useradd', 'adduser', or by editing passwd/shadow. Behavior chain includes execution of user management binaries or modification of user database files.

mutableElements.description: Account creation may be scripted via shell scripts, cron jobs, or remote shells
Flag if commands are issued from remote sessions (e.g., sshd)

description.en: Account creation using 'dscl -create' or via GUI tools. Detection involves command execution and file changes to the local directory services database.

mutableElements.description: Accounts like 'svc', 'backup' may blend into legit naming patterns
Identify if dscl was run locally, via ARD, or Terminal.app

description.en: Account created using esxcli commands. Sequence includes esxcli execution and successful modification to account DB.

mutableElements.description: Console sessions vs SSH vs vSphere CLI session may affect alert fidelity

description.en: Account created in a running container (e.g., via 'useradd' or by modifying /etc/passwd directly). Detectable via runtime telemetry (e.g., Falco or eBPF hooks).

mutableElements.description: Distinguish between ephemeral containers and long-lived service containers
Determine if account was added inside host, user, or PID namespace

description.en: Account created via CLI using 'username' command or REST API. Detectable through AAA logging or CLI history telemetry.

mutableElements.description: Some devices allow unprivileged user creation—adjust based on role risk
Creation via Telnet, SSH, or serial console affects detection priority

brief.en: Adversaries may create a domain account to maintain access to victim systems. Domain accounts are those managed by Active Directory Domain Services where access and permissions are configured across systems and services that are part of that domain. Domain accounts can cover user, administrator, and service accounts.

description.en: Adversary uses built-in tools such as 'net user /add /domain' or PowerShell to create a domain user account. The behavior chain includes: (1) suspicious process execution on a domain controller followed by (2) user account creation event (Event ID 4720) on the same host.

mutableElements.description: Detection triggers when Event ID 4720 follows a suspicious process within 2 minutes.
Allow filtering of known admin tools vs adversarial misuse (e.g., net.exe, powershell.exe).
Filter accounts with domain admin privileges creating new users vs standard helpdesk roles.
Restrict to only domain controller hosts to reduce noise from workstations.

description.en: Adversary with access to domain management tools (e.g., realmd, samba-tool, ldapmodify) creates a new domain user via command-line utilities. Behavior chain: LDAP command or script triggers → user entry added in AD via Kerberos/LDAP traffic.

logSources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
logSources.channel: execution of realmd, samba-tool, or ldapmodify with user-related arguments

logSources.name: NSM:Flow
logSources.channel: TGS-REQ and AS-REQ seen for new user shortly after domain-modifying process

mutableElements.description: realmd, samba-tool, ldapmodify or custom script
Expected Kerberos traffic from new domain account within X minutes of command
Script execution from interactive shell vs scheduled task

description.en: macOS clients joined to AD via LDAP may script account provisioning via dsconfigad, dscl, or LDAP scripts. Detection occurs when such tools run on a domain-joined system, followed by authentication attempts by a previously unseen account.

logSources.name: macos:unifiedlog
logSources.channel: dsconfigad or dscl with create or append options for AD-bound users

mutableElements.description: Only flag on AD-bound systems with valid LDAP context
Distinguish between user accounts and computer accounts

brief.en: Adversaries may create a cloud account to maintain access to victim systems. With a sufficient level of access, such accounts may be used to establish secondary credentialed access that does not require persistent remote access tools to be deployed on the system. In addition to user accounts, cloud accounts may be associated with services. Cloud providers handle the concept of service accounts in different ways.

description.en: Adversaries create user accounts via identity provider APIs or admin portals (e.g., Azure AD, Okta). These accounts may be assigned elevated privileges or used in chained authentication. Detection monitors Add User activity from suspicious IPs or automation sources, followed by role/permission escalation.

mutableElements.description: Filter on IPs outside known admin networks or geographies
Raise alert if total admins exceeds historical baseline
Differentiate between user and service principal creation

description.en: Adversaries use cloud API, CLI, or console to create IAM users or roles. Initial CreateUser is followed by policy/role attachment. Detection monitors temporal chains involving IAM:CreateUser, AttachUserPolicy, and credential generation, especially from automation or foreign IP ranges.

mutableElements.description: Alert when creation happens in unexpected regions
Chain CreateUser → AttachPolicy → AccessKey within short timeframe
Monitor API calls from non-console or automation tools

description.en: Adversaries create SaaS accounts via admin dashboards or integrations (e.g., Zoom, Salesforce, Slack). Monitor lifecycle.create or account provisioning events from non-standard sources or times.

mutableElements.description: Trigger only for high-privilege or sensitive applications
Compare actor to list of approved SaaS administrators

description.en: Adversaries leverage M365 or Google Workspace APIs to create users, service accounts, or guest accounts. Follow-on behaviors include login activity, role escalation, or service principal token generation.

mutableElements.description: Only alert on additions to high-value groups (e.g., Domain Admins)
Tune alerts based on guest vs internal user creation

brief.en: Adversaries may leverage Microsoft Office-based applications for persistence between startups. Microsoft Office is a fairly common application suite on Windows-based operating systems within an enterprise network. There are multiple mechanisms that can be used with Office for persistence when an Office-based application is started; this can include the use of Office Template Macros and add-ins.

description.en: Office-based persistence via Office template macros, Outlook forms/rules/homepage, or registry-persistent scripts. Adversary modifies registry keys or Office application directories to load malicious scripts at startup.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Application
logSources.channel: Outlook rule creation, form load, or homepage redirection

mutableElements.description: Tune based on expected Office process tree (e.g., WINWORD.EXE spawning cmd.exe)
Specific keys related to Office startup such as Outlook Today, AddIns, or Template Macros
Window of process execution after user login or Outlook launch
Detect persistence within high-value user mailboxes (e.g., admin, finance, C-suite)

description.en: Startup-based persistence mechanisms within Microsoft Office Suite like template macros and home page redirects being configured through internal automation or client-side settings.

logSources.name: m365:mailboxaudit
logSources.channel: Outlook rule creation or custom form deployment

mutableElements.description: Identify rule actions that execute scripts, forward emails externally, or start external content
Focus on users with sensitive roles or shared mailboxes
Detect persistence artifacts created shortly after credential access or login from an unusual location

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office templates to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Microsoft Office contains templates that are part of common Office applications and are used to customize styles. The base templates within the application are used each time an application starts.

description.en: Adversaries inject VBA macros into Office templates such as Normal.dotm or Personal.xlsb or redirect Office template load path via registry key (GlobalDotName) to gain persistence. Template macros trigger execution of malicious code on application startup.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Microsoft-Office-Alerts
logSources.channel: Office application warning or alert on macro execution from template

mutableElements.description: Path to Normal.dotm, Personal.xlsb, or Excel/Word startup templates may vary by Office version and user
GlobalDotName or equivalent registry keys may differ across Office versions or deployments
Office process creation and macro execution timing after system or user login
May be scoped to high-value users or those with access to sensitive templates

description.en: Malicious VBA macros embedded in base templates like Normal.dotm or Personal.xlsb are automatically loaded and executed at startup. Template path may be hijacked to load a remote or attacker-controlled template via GlobalDotName registry setting.

mutableElements.description: Macros may be embedded in local user templates or retrieved from shared network paths
Macro execution policy (disabled, warn, enabled) varies by tenant or user configuration

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse the Microsoft Office "Office Test" Registry key to obtain persistence on a compromised system. An Office Test Registry location exists that allows a user to specify an arbitrary DLL that will be executed every time an Office application is started. This Registry key is thought to be used by Microsoft to load DLLs for testing and debugging purposes while developing Office applications.

description.en: Adversaries create the 'Office Test\Special\Perf' registry key and specify a malicious DLL path that is auto-loaded when an Office application starts. This DLL is injected into the Office process memory space and can provide persistent execution without requiring macro enablement.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Microsoft-Office-Alerts
logSources.channel: Unexpected DLL or component loaded at Office startup

mutableElements.description: Path to 'Office test\Special\Perf' may vary by Office version, 32/64-bit, or architecture (HKCU vs HKLM)
Injected DLL may reside in different user-writable locations (e.g., %APPDATA%, %TEMP%, or network shares)
Process name (e.g., winword.exe, excel.exe) may vary by Office deployment and usage
Time between DLL registry creation and first Office execution may vary depending on user activity
Malicious DLL may target only specific users, necessitating correlation with interactive logon sessions

description.en: Office application auto-loads a non-standard DLL during startup triggered via Office Test Registry key, often without macro warning banners. DLL persistence mechanism circumvents traditional macro defenses.

logSources.name: m365:unified
logSources.channel: Non-standard Office startup component detected (e.g., unexpected DLL path)

mutableElements.description: DLL may be placed in location trusted by Office configuration or signed to evade alerts
Only specific tenants or users may have Office auditing enabled at granular DLL load level

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook forms to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook forms are used as templates for presentation and functionality in Outlook messages. Custom Outlook forms can be created that will execute code when a specifically crafted email is sent by an adversary utilizing the same custom Outlook form.

description.en: Adversary uses a tool like Ruler to insert a malicious custom form into the user's Outlook mailbox. The form is designed to auto-execute on Outlook startup or on receipt of a specially crafted email. This results in child processes launched from outlook.exe and possibly network connections or payload loading.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Application
logSources.channel: Outlook errors loading or processing custom form templates

logSources.name: WinEventLog:PowerShell
logSources.channel: Execution of Microsoft script to enumerate custom forms in Outlook mailbox

mutableElements.description: Malicious forms may be stored in various user-specific locations in the Outlook mailbox (e.g., IPM.Note class)
Child process spawned by outlook.exe may vary (e.g., powershell.exe, rundll32.exe, mshta.exe)
Form-triggered execution may happen immediately upon Outlook startup or with delay after crafted message arrival
Form behavior and error logs may vary across Outlook 2013, 2016, and M365 builds
Attack may target only specific users; contextual correlation needed for account baselining

description.en: Outlook form execution upon message receipt or client launch results in automated code execution within user session. Form definitions deviate from standard templates and include script logic or COM object calls embedded in form fields.

logSources.name: m365:unified
logSources.channel: Unusual form activity within Outlook client, including load of non-default forms

mutableElements.description: Not all tenants may enable audit logs of custom form activity or COM component usage in Office

Frequency of form triggers may be anomalously high compared to baseline Outlook usage

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook's Home Page feature to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook Home Page is a legacy feature used to customize the presentation of Outlook folders. This feature allows for an internal or external URL to be loaded and presented whenever a folder is opened. A malicious HTML page can be crafted that will execute code when loaded by Outlook Home Page.

description.en: Adversary uses a tool like Ruler to configure a malicious Outlook folder Home Page that loads a remote or embedded HTML payload upon folder interaction. Execution chain begins with Outlook launching, a specific folder being accessed, and a suspicious child process being spawned or COM-based execution invoked.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Application
logSources.channel: Outlook logs indicating failure to load or render HTML page in Home Page view

logSources.name: WinEventLog:PowerShell
logSources.channel: Execution of PowerShell script to enumerate or remove malicious Home Page folder config

mutableElements.description: Home Page can be configured on any folder like Calendar, Inbox, or custom folders
The Home Page URL may point to internal or external content, hosted on trusted or unknown domains
Execution may result in launch of scripting hosts (e.g., mshta.exe, wscript.exe) from outlook.exe
Execution may occur only when the specific folder is accessed after launch, not immediately at startup
Behavior may vary if the folder's form view is customized or suppressed via GPO

description.en: Malicious HTML or script is rendered as a Home Page for a specific Outlook folder. Outlook accesses that folder, loads remote content, and executes embedded JavaScript or ActiveX/COM logic resulting in unauthorized actions or local execution.

logSources.name: m365:unified
logSources.channel: Folder configuration updated with external or HTML-formatted Home Page via Set-MailboxFolder

logSources.name: m365:messagetrace
logSources.channel: Inbound email triggering Outlook to auto-access folder tied to malicious Home Page

mutableElements.description: Home Page customization may not be audited unless detailed message or folder auditing is enabled
Anomalous access to folders not usually interacted with can signal triggering of malicious view
Mail clients may restrict remote Home Page content unless domain is explicitly allowed

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Outlook rules to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Outlook rules allow a user to define automated behavior to manage email messages. A benign rule might, for example, automatically move an email to a particular folder in Outlook if it contains specific words from a specific sender.

description.en: Adversary uses a tool like Ruler or MFCMapi to create a malicious Outlook rule that triggers execution upon receipt of a crafted email. On email delivery, Outlook executes the rule, resulting in code execution (e.g., launching mshta.exe or PowerShell). Outlook spawns a non-standard child process, often unsanctioned, without user interaction.

logSources.name: WinEventLog:Application
logSources.channel: Outlook rule execution failure or abnormal rule execution context

logSources.name: WinEventLog:PowerShell
logSources.channel: PowerShell launched from outlook.exe or triggered without user invocation

mutableElements.description: Outlook may spawn mshta.exe, powershell.exe, or wscript.exe depending on attacker payload
Rule execution may depend on message subject, sender, or message header content
Legitimate Outlook activity should not spawn scripting or interpreter processes
Execution may occur with delay after message receipt or folder interaction

description.en: Adversary adds a new Outlook rule with modified or obfuscated PRRULEMSGNAME and PRRULEMSGPROVIDER attributes using MFCMapi or Ruler. Rule is triggered when email arrives, executing embedded or external code. Mailbox audit logs or Unified Audit Log shows automated rule-triggered action without user interaction.

logSources.name: m365:unified
logSources.channel: Creation or modification of inbox rule outside of normal user behavior

logSources.name: m365:messagetrace
logSources.channel: Inbound email matches crafted rule trigger pattern tied to persistence logic

mutableElements.description: Mailbox rule changes may not be captured unless advanced audit logging is enabled
Malicious rules may use spoofed or non-standard PRRULEMSGPROVIDER values
Triggering emails may contain uncommon but benign-looking subjects
Target user account may be inactive or high-value (e.g., VIP, service account)

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse Microsoft Office add-ins to obtain persistence on a compromised system. Office add-ins can be used to add functionality to Office programs.

description.en: An adversary writes or drops a malicious Office Add-in (e.g., WLL, XLL, COM) to a trusted directory or modifies registry keys to load malicious add-ins on Office application launch. Upon user opening Word or Excel, the add-in is automatically loaded, triggering execution of the payload, often spawning scripting engines or anomalous child processes.

mutableElements.description: Malicious add-ins may have varying extensions (.wll, .xll, .dll, .vsto)
Office trusted add-in paths may differ across enterprise configurations
Registry keys used to load add-ins may be version- and app-specific
Office processes spawning mshta.exe, powershell.exe, or rundll32.exe are abnormal
Add-in loading may occur only during Office launch windows

description.en: Malicious Office add-ins loaded via VSTO, COM, or VBA auto-load paths. Upon launch of Word/Excel/Outlook, the add-in executes code without user action. Add-in resides in trusted directory or registered via Office COM/VBE subsystem. Behavior includes unsigned add-in execution, anomalous load context, or add-in spawning interpreter process.

mutableElements.description: Admins may allow or block unsigned add-ins depending on GPO configuration
Different Office versions store trusted paths and add-in configs in version-specific locations
Some add-ins only load on specific actions (new document, open file, etc.)

brief.en: Adversaries may use Obfuscated Files or Information to hide artifacts of an intrusion from analysis. They may require separate mechanisms to decode or deobfuscate that information depending on how they intend to use it. Methods for doing that include built-in functionality of malware or by using utilities present on the system.

description.en: An adversary leverages built-in tools such as certutil.exe, powershell.exe, or copy.exe to decode, reassemble, or extract hidden malicious content from obfuscated containers or encoded formats. The decoding utility often spawns shortly after file staging or download and may be chained with script interpreters or further payload execution.

mutableElements.description: May vary across environments (e.g., certutil, powershell, copy, expand, 7zip)
Targets may use .txt, .cer, .enc, .b64, .zip, etc. to disguise payloads
Command syntax varies between base64 decoding, copy /b, and expand switches
Deobfuscation typically follows staging/download within a short timeframe

description.en: The adversary uses native utilities like base64, gzip, tar, or openssl to decode, decompress, or decrypt files that were previously staged or downloaded. These tools may be chained with curl/wget and executed via bash/zsh, often to extract an embedded payload or reverse shell script.

logSources.name: auditd:SYSCALL
logSources.channel: bash/zsh of base64, tar, gzip, or openssl immediately after file write

mutableElements.description: Shell interpreter may vary (bash, zsh, dash, sh)
May include base64, openssl, gunzip, tar, uudecode
Expected parent process may vary in attacker chain (e.g., curl, bash, ssh)
Detection regex should support flexible patterning of decode switches

description.en: The adversary invokes built-in scripting or decoding tools like base64, plutil, or AppleScript-based utilities to decode files embedded in staging artifacts. Decoding often occurs post-download or as part of post-exploitation payload deployment via zsh, python, or osascript.

logSources.name: macos:unifiedlog
logSources.channel: base64 -d or osascript invoked on staged file

mutableElements.description: Could involve base64, osascript, python, perl, or plutil
Deobfuscation may happen within GUI app context or LaunchAgent/Daemon
May differ depending on local user, root escalation, or persistence method

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse software extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Software extensions are modular components that enhance or customize the functionality of software applications, including web browsers, Integrated Development Environments (IDEs), and other platforms.

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse internet browser extensions to establish persistent access to victim systems. Browser extensions or plugins are small programs that can add functionality to and customize aspects of internet browsers.

description.en: Installation of a new browser extension followed by suspicious file writes or outbound network connections to untrusted domains by the browser process.

mutableElements.description: Extension installation by privileged or domain users may require higher scrutiny
Custom or portable browsers may not match default paths
Installation paths may vary by version or user profile

mutableElements.description: Different versions may store extensions in variant preference folders
May vary with OS version; some install flags deprecated in macOS 11+

Custom list of suspicious destination domains for browser traffic

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse an integrated development environment (IDE) extension to establish persistent access to victim systems. IDEs such as Visual Studio Code, IntelliJ IDEA, and Eclipse support extensions - software components that add features like code linting, auto-completion, task automation, or integration with tools like Git and Docker. A malicious extension can be installed through an extension marketplace (i.

description.en: Adversary installs or side-loads an IDE extension (VS Code, IntelliJ/JetBrains, Eclipse) or enables IDE tunneling. Chain: (1) IDE binary starts on a non-developer endpoint or server, often with install/force/tunnel flags → (2) extension files/registrations appear under user profile → (3) browser/IDE initiates outbound connections to extension marketplaces, update endpoints, or IDE remote/tunnel services → (4) optional child tools (ssh, node, powershell) execute under the IDE context.

mutableElements.description: Executable names/paths (e.g., code.exe, idea64.exe, eclipse.exe, jetbrains-gateway.exe) vary by version and packaging.
Flags such as --install-extension, --force, --disable-extensions, --user-data-dir, --uninstall-extension, tunnel/remote flags are tunable.
List of hosts where IDEs should never run (prod servers, DCs).
Approved extension marketplaces/ide services; use to suppress benign traffic.
Correlation horizon (e.g., 15–30m) between process start, file writes, and outbound IDE/tunnel connections.

description.en: Adversary installs or abuses IDE extensions via CLI or direct write to profile directories and then communicates with marketplaces or remote tunnel services. Chain: auditd execve (code/idea/eclipse) with install/update flags or writes under ~/.vscode/extensions, ~/.config/JetBrains → outbound flows to .visualstudio.com, marketplace.visualstudio.com, .jetbrains.com, githubusercontent.com, or SSH/WebSocket tunnel endpoints → optional ssh/node processes spawned by IDE.

Enterprise-approved repos and proxies to reduce FPs.
Limit to non-developer users or production servers.
Join horizon across file, process, and network telemetry.

description.en: Adversary adds IDE extensions or plugins (VS Code, JetBrains Toolbox/EAP, Eclipse) via GUI or CLI, possibly via managed profiles. Chain: process start with install/update flags → plist/extension folder changes under ~/Library/Application Support/Code or ~/Library/Application Support/JetBrains → outbound connections to marketplaces/tunnel services → optional helper (ssh/node) spawned.

logSources.name: macos:unifiedlog

Correlation range between install and first beacon.

brief.en: Adversaries may take advantage of security vulnerabilities and inherent functionality in browser software to change content, modify user-behaviors, and intercept information as part of various browser session hijacking techniques.

description.en: Adversary gains high integrity or special privileges (e.g., SeDebugPrivilege), locates a running browser process, opens it with write/inject rights, and modifies it (e.g., CreateRemoteThread / DLL load) to inherit cookies/tokens or establish a browser pivot. Optional step: create a new logon session or use explicit credentials, then drive the victim browser to intranet resources.

mutableElements.description: Set of monitored browsers (chrome.exe, msedge.exe, firefox.exe, iexplore.exe). Adjust per fleet.
Access rights implying injection (e.g., 0x1FFFFF, 0x1F3FF, VMWRITE, VMOPERATION, CREATETHREAD). Tune by EDR mapping.
Allowed module signers within browser processes (e.g., Microsoft, Google). Helps flag unsigned/unknown ImageLoad into browsers.
Enterprise internal ranges or DNS suffixes to identify intranet pivoting via the browser.
Correlation interval (e.g., 10–20 minutes) linking privilege gain → access → modification → network usage.
Legitimate tools that may automate browsers (e.g., Selenium drivers). Reduce FPs by allowlisting.

brief.en: Adversaries may gather credential material by invoking or forcing a user to automatically provide authentication information through a mechanism in which they can intercept. brief.en: Adversaries may attempt to access detailed information about the password policy used within an enterprise network or cloud environment. Password policies are a way to enforce complex passwords that are difficult to guess or crack through Brute Force. This information may help the adversary to create a list of common passwords and launch dictionary and/or brute force attacks which adheres to the policy (e.g.

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse utilities that allow for command execution to bypass security restrictions that limit the use of command-line interpreters. Various Windows utilities may be used to execute commands, possibly without invoking cmd. For example, Forfiles, the Program Compatibility Assistant (pcalua.exe), components of the Windows Subsystem for Linux (WSL), Scriptrunner.

description.en: Cause→effect chain: (1) A user or service launches an indirection utility (e.g., forfiles.exe, pcalua.exe, wsl.exe, scriptrunner.exe, ssh.exe with -o ProxyCommand/LocalCommand). (2) That utility spawns a secondary program/command (PowerShell, cmd, msiexec, regsvr32, curl, arbitrary EXE) and/or opens outbound network connections. (3) Optional precursor modification of SSH config to persist LocalCommand/ProxyCommand. Correlate process creation, command/script content, file access to %USERPROFILE%\.ssh\config, and network connections from the utility or its child.

brief.en: Adversaries may exploit software vulnerabilities in client applications to execute code. Vulnerabilities can exist in software due to unsecure coding practices that can lead to unanticipated behavior. Adversaries can take advantage of certain vulnerabilities through targeted exploitation for the purpose of arbitrary code execution.

description.en: Cause→effect chain: (1) A client app (browser, Office, PDF/Flash/reader) experiences a crash/abnormal exit or loads from an unusual location, then (2) drops or modifies a file in user-writable paths, and/or (3) spawns an unexpected child (e.g., powershell/cmd/mshta/rundll32/wscript/installer), and (4) establishes outbound C2-like connections shortly after. Correlate application logs, file writes, process lineage, and network egress within a short window.

brief.en: An adversary may rely upon specific actions by a user in order to gain execution. Users may be subjected to social engineering to get them to execute malicious code by, for example, opening a malicious document file or link. These user actions will typically be observed as follow-on behavior from forms of Phishing.

Adversaries may use several types of files that require a user to execute them, including .doc, .pdf, .xls, .rtf, .scr, .exe, .

Shortly after start, the container spawns unexpected utilities (e.g., curl/wget/bash/python), or makes outbound network connections atypical for the namespace/workload. The analytic correlates Image Creation/Download → Container Creation → Container Start → Command Execution/Network activity within a short window and with a consistent image digest.

brief.en: Adversaries may register a rogue Domain Controller to enable manipulation of Active Directory data. DCShadow may be used to create a rogue Domain Controller (DC). DCShadow is a method of manipulating Active Directory (AD) data, including objects and schemas, by registering (or reusing an inactive registration) and simulating the behavior of a DC.

These events in combination, especially from hosts outside the Domain Controllers OU, may indicate DCShadow or rogue DC activity.

brief.en: Adversaries may exploit remote services to gain unauthorized access to internal systems once inside of a network. brief.en: Adversaries may use trusted scripts, often signed with certificates, to proxy the execution of malicious files. This behavior may be abused by adversaries to execute malicious files that could bypass application control and signature validation on systems.

Control Panel items are registered executable (.exe) or Control Panel (.cpl) files, the latter are actually renamed dynamic-link library (.

The Microsoft Connection Manager Profile Installer (CMSTP.exe) is a command-line program used to install Connection Manager service profiles. Msiexec.exe is the command-line utility for the Windows Installer and is thus commonly associated with executing installation packages (.msi). The Msiexec.exe binary may also be digitally signed by Microsoft. Adversaries may abuse msiexec.exe to launch local or network accessible MSI files. Msiexec.exe can also execute DLLs.

Odbcconf.exe is a Windows utility that allows you to configure Open Database Connectivity (ODBC) drivers and data source names. The Odbcconf.exe binary may be digitally signed by Microsoft. Adversaries may abuse odbcconf.exe to bypass application control solutions that do not account for its potential abuse. Similar to Regsvr32, odbcconf.

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse components of Terminal Services to enable persistent access to systems. Microsoft Terminal Services, renamed to Remote Desktop Services in some Windows Server OSs as of 2022, enable remote terminal connections to hosts. Terminal Services allows servers to transmit a full, interactive, graphical user interface to clients via RDP. Windows Services that are run as a "generic" process (ex: svchost.

brief.en: Adversaries may abuse vSphere Installation Bundles (VIBs) to establish persistent access to ESXi hypervisors. VIBs are collections of files used for software distribution and virtual system management in VMware environments. Since ESXi uses an in-memory filesystem where changes made to most files are stored in RAM rather than in persistent storage, these modifications are lost after a reboot.

brief.en: Adversaries may shutdown/reboot systems to interrupt access to, or aid in the destruction of, those systems. Cloud service providers often provide infrastructure throughout the world in order to improve performance, provide redundancy, and allow customers to meet compliance requirements.

TFTP boot (netbooting) is commonly used by network administrators to load configuration-controlled network device images from a centralized management server. Netbooting is one option in the boot sequence and can be used to centralize, manage, and control device images.

description.en: Detection of unauthorized changes to boot configurations pointing to TFTP servers, unusual firmware loads during netbooting, or suspicious TFTP traffic. Correlation of boot config modifications, command history logs, and unexpected system image hashes provides detection coverage for adversaries attempting to persist via malicious TFTP boot images.

brief.en: Adversaries may create or modify system-level processes to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. brief.en: Adversaries may create or modify launch agents to repeatedly execute malicious payloads as part of persistence. Launch Daemons are plist files used to interact with Launchd, the service management framework used by macOS. Launch Daemons require elevated privileges to install, are executed for every user on a system prior to login, and run in the background without the need for user interaction.

Detectable through correlated Unified Logs, file monitoring, and process telemetry.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence and/or elevate privileges using system mechanisms that trigger execution based on specific events. Various operating systems have means to monitor and subscribe to events such as logons or other user activity such as running specific applications/binaries.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by a file type association. When a file is opened, the default program used to open the file (also called the file association or handler) is checked.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by user inactivity. Screensavers are programs that execute after a configurable time of user inactivity and consist of Portable Executable (PE) files with a .scr file extension. The Windows screensaver application scrnsave.

description.en: Unusual screensaver (.scr) executions correlated with recent registry modifications to HKCU\Control Panel\Desktop values such as SCRNSAVE.exe, ScreenSaveTimeout, and ScreenSaveActive. Detection focuses on PE image paths not consistent with known legitimate screensavers and triggered after user inactivity timeout.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence and elevate privileges by executing malicious content triggered by a Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) event subscription. WMI can be used to install event filters, providers, consumers, and bindings that execute code when a defined event occurs. Examples of events that may be subscribed to are the wall clock time, user login, or the computer's uptime.

Detect command-line execution of mofcomp.exe, usage of Register-WmiEvent via PowerShell, and anomalous child processes of WmiPrvSE.exe that indicate triggered execution. Look for lateral anomalies in process lineage and WMI logging channels.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence through executing malicious commands triggered by a user’s shell. User Unix Shells execute several configuration scripts at different points throughout the session based on events. For example, when a user opens a command-line interface or remotely logs in (such as via SSH) a login shell is initiated.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by an interrupt signal. The trap command allows programs and shells to specify commands that will be executed upon receiving interrupt signals. A common situation is a script allowing for graceful termination and handling of common keyboard interrupts like ctrl+c and ctrl+d.

description.en: Correlate file modifications in shell startup scripts (e.g., .bashrc, .profile) with embedded trap commands and observe if those changes are followed by the unexpected execution of child processes when terminal signals (e.g., SIGINT) are triggered. Use contextual linking with user session activity to detect privilege misuse.

brief.en: Adversaries may establish persistence by executing malicious content triggered by the execution of tainted binaries. Mach-O binaries have a series of headers that are used to perform certain operations when a binary is loaded. The LCLOADDYLIB header in a Mach-O binary tells macOS and OS X which dynamic libraries (dylibs) to load during execution time.
